questions.exp: A tax return preparer is any person who prepares for compensation, or employs others to prepare for compensation, all or a substantial portion of a return or refund claim. Uncompensated preparers, employees preparing their employer's return, and providers of mechanical assistance such as software are excluded.

questions.q: Ames transferred land with an adjusted basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $100,000 to a newly formed corporation in exchange for stock worth $80,000 and $20,000 cash. Immediately afterward Ames owned 85% of the corporation's only class of stock. How much gain must Ames recognize?
questions.exp: Realized gain is $100,000 − $30,000 = $70,000, but under §351 gain is recognized only to the extent of boot received, so the recognized gain is the lesser of $70,000 or the $20,000 cash. Recognizing the full $70,000 ignores §351 nonrecognition, which applies because Ames has 80% control.

questions.q: Using the same facts (land basis $30,000, FMV $100,000, exchanged for $80,000 of stock and $20,000 cash in a qualifying §351 transfer, $20,000 gain recognized), what is Ames's basis in the stock received?
questions.exp: Under §358, stock basis = $30,000 property basis + $20,000 gain recognized − $20,000 cash received = $30,000. Using the stock's $80,000 fair market value is the common mistake; the deferred $50,000 gain is preserved in the lower basis.

questions.q: Wade transferred machinery with an adjusted basis of $45,000 and a fair market value of $90,000 to his controlled corporation for stock worth $75,000 and $15,000 cash in a transaction qualifying under §351. What is the corporation's basis in the machinery?
questions.exp: Wade recognizes gain equal to the $15,000 boot (realized gain $45,000), and the corporation's basis is the transferor's basis plus gain recognized: $45,000 + $15,000 = $60,000 (§362). The corporation does not take a $90,000 fair market value basis in a §351 transfer.

questions.q: Baker transferred a building with an adjusted basis of $40,000 and a fair market value of $150,000, subject to a $60,000 mortgage, to a corporation in exchange for all of its stock. The corporation assumed the mortgage, and there was no tax-avoidance purpose. How much gain does Baker recognize?
questions.exp: Under §357, liabilities assumed in excess of the aggregate basis of property transferred produce gain: $60,000 − $40,000 = $20,000. Liability assumption is normally not boot, so answering $0 overlooks the excess-liability rule.

questions.q: Cole transferred equipment with an adjusted basis of $80,000 and a fair market value of $200,000, subject to a $50,000 liability, to a corporation for stock worth $150,000. The corporation assumed the liability, Cole has 100% control, and there was a bona fide business purpose. What is Cole's basis in the stock?
questions.exp: No gain is recognized because the $50,000 liability does not exceed the $80,000 basis, but the liability assumed is treated as money received for basis purposes: $80,000 − $50,000 = $30,000 (§358). Ignoring the liability gives $80,000.

questions.q: Dahl transferred property worth $70,000 to a new corporation for 70 shares, and Eng received 30 shares worth $30,000 solely for services rendered in organizing the corporation. These were the only shares issued. What is the tax result?
choices: Neither Dahl nor Eng recognizes income because §351 applies to the incorporation
Dahl recognizes his realized gain on the property, and Eng recognizes $30,000 of ordinary income
Dahl recognizes no gain, and Eng recognizes $30,000 of capital gain
Dahl recognizes no gain, and Eng recognizes $30,000 of ordinary income
questions.exp: Stock received solely for services is not counted toward the 80% control test, so the property transferors own only 70% and §351 fails; Dahl's realized gain is taxable. Eng has $30,000 of ordinary compensation income in any event.

questions.q: For purposes of §351, control means ownership immediately after the exchange of stock possessing at least:
choices: 80% of the total value of all classes of stock
50% of the voting power and 50% of the value of all stock
More than 50% of the voting power of all classes of stock
80% of the total combined voting power and 80% of the total number of shares of each class of nonvoting stock
questions.exp: Section 368 defines control as at least 80% of the total combined voting power of all voting stock and at least 80% of the total number of shares of each other class of stock. The test is not based on the value of the stock.

questions.q: Which statement about holding periods in a §351 transfer of a capital asset in exchange for stock only is correct?
choices: The shareholder tacks the asset's holding period onto the stock, and the corporation tacks the shareholder's holding period onto the asset
The corporation's holding period in the asset begins on the date of the exchange
Neither the shareholder nor the corporation may tack a prior holding period
The shareholder's holding period in the stock begins on the date of the exchange
questions.exp: Stock received for a capital or §1231 asset takes a holding period that includes the asset's holding period (§1223(1)), and the corporation's carryover-basis property includes the transferor's holding period (§1223(2)). Tacking for the shareholder would not apply if the property were inventory.

questions.q: Fern Corp. issued 1,000 shares of its own newly issued common stock in exchange for land worth $250,000. Fern's shares had no prior basis. How much gain does Fern Corp. recognize?
choices: $250,000, because Fern's basis in its new shares is zero
Gain equal to the excess of the land's value over its par value
$0, because a corporation recognizes no gain or loss on issuing its own stock for property
$250,000 of capital gain, deferred until Fern sells the land
questions.exp: Under §1032 a corporation recognizes no gain or loss on receiving money or property in exchange for its own stock, whether or not §351 applies to the transferor. The zero basis of newly issued shares is irrelevant.

questions.q: Gray transferred property to her controlled corporation, and the corporation assumed a liability that Gray had incurred shortly before the transfer for the principal purpose of avoiding federal income tax. How is the liability treated?
choices: It is ignored for both gain and basis purposes
The entire liability is treated as money received (boot) by Gray
It is treated as a contribution to capital by the corporation
Only the portion of the liability exceeding Gray's basis is treated as boot
questions.exp: Under the §357 tax-avoidance rule, if the principal purpose of a liability assumption is tax avoidance or lacks a bona fide business purpose, the total amount of all liabilities assumed is treated as money received. The excess-over-basis rule is a separate provision of §357.

questions.q: Hale transferred equipment with an adjusted basis of $100,000 and a fair market value of $70,000 to a corporation solely for stock in a transaction qualifying under §351. Hale made no election under §362(e)(2)(C). What is the corporation's basis in the equipment?
questions.exp: When the aggregate basis of property a transferor contributes exceeds its aggregate fair market value, §362(e)(2) limits the corporation's basis to fair market value, $70,000, while Hale keeps a $100,000 stock basis. A $100,000 carryover basis would duplicate the built-in loss.

questions.q: Ivey transferred property with an adjusted basis of $50,000 and a fair market value of $40,000 to her controlled corporation for stock worth $30,000 and $10,000 cash. What is Ivey's basis in the stock?
questions.exp: No loss is recognized in a §351 exchange even when boot is received (§351), so stock basis = $50,000 − $10,000 cash + $0 gain = $40,000. Using the stock's $30,000 value incorrectly treats the transaction as taxable.

questions.q: Jory transferred land (basis $10,000, FMV $40,000) and also performed services worth $10,000 in exchange for stock worth $50,000. Jory's transfer of property qualifies under §351. What is Jory's basis in the stock?
questions.exp: Jory recognizes $10,000 of ordinary income for the stock received for services, and that income is added to basis: $10,000 land basis + $10,000 compensation income = $20,000. The $30,000 gain on the land is deferred, so using full value of $50,000 is wrong.

questions.q: Kim owns all 100 outstanding shares of Kay Corp. Lee transfers appreciated property to Kay Corp. for 150 newly issued shares; Kim transfers nothing. What is the tax consequence to Lee?
choices: No gain, because Kay Corp. is controlled by its shareholders after the exchange
Lee recognizes gain only to the extent his shares exceed 50% of the stock
Lee recognizes his realized gain, because the transferors own only 60% immediately after the exchange
No gain, because §351 applies whenever new shares are issued for property
questions.exp: Only stock held by transferors counts toward control; Lee owns 150 ÷ 250 = 60%, short of 80%, so the exchange is taxable to Lee. Kim could be counted only by also transferring property of more than relatively small value.

questions.q: Lund transferred equipment with an original cost of $50,000, an adjusted basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $45,000 to his controlled corporation for stock worth $40,000 and $5,000 cash. What is the amount and character of Lund's recognized gain?
choices: $25,000 ordinary income
$5,000 ordinary income
$5,000 capital gain
questions.exp: Recognized gain is limited to the $5,000 boot (realized gain $25,000), and because recognized gain does not exceed the $30,000 of prior depreciation, it is ordinary §1245 recapture. The unrecognized recapture carries over to the corporation.

questions.q: A married couple filing jointly sold §1244 stock they had acquired at original issuance for $180,000 for $30,000. The corporation met all §1244 requirements. How is the $150,000 loss treated?
choices: $3,000 ordinary loss and $147,000 capital loss carryover
$100,000 ordinary loss and $50,000 capital loss
$150,000 ordinary loss
$50,000 ordinary loss and $100,000 capital loss
questions.exp: Section 1244 allows an ordinary loss of up to $100,000 per year on a joint return ($50,000 for other filers); the remaining $50,000 is capital loss. Reversing the two amounts applies the single-filer limit to the wrong portion.

questions.q: Which statement about §1244 stock is correct?
choices: Only an individual (or partnership) that acquired the stock at original issuance from the corporation may claim the ordinary loss
A corporate shareholder may claim the ordinary loss
Gain on the sale of §1244 stock is also ordinary
Any later purchaser of the stock may claim the ordinary loss
questions.exp: The §1244 ordinary loss is available only to the original individual holder (or a partnership that was the original holder, passed through to individual partners) of stock issued for money or property. Gains on §1244 stock remain capital, and later purchasers and corporations do not qualify.

questions.q: In a transaction otherwise qualifying under §351, Mona received stock and a 10-year note issued by the corporation. How is the note treated?
choices: As ordinary income equal to its face amount
As boot, taxable to the extent of Mona's realized gain
As stock, because it is a long-term security
As a nontaxable return of capital
questions.exp: Since 1989, §351 protects only stock; debt securities of any term are boot, and gain is recognized up to their value (with possible installment reporting). Treating long-term securities as stock reflects pre-1989 law.

questions.q: In a §351 exchange, Nash Corp. transferred land it held (basis $5,000, FMV $15,000) to a transferor as part of the consideration, along with Nash stock. What does Nash Corp. recognize?
choices: $10,000 gain, because a corporation recognizes gain on transferring appreciated property other than its own stock
No gain, because the land is boot only to the shareholder
$15,000 gain equal to the land's fair market value
No gain, because §1032 protects the corporation
questions.exp: Section 351 applies §311 rules, so the corporation recognizes gain on appreciated boot property it transfers: $15,000 − $5,000 = $10,000. Section 1032 covers only the corporation's own stock.

questions.q: Ortiz, the sole shareholder of Ortiz Corp., contributed $40,000 cash to the corporation without receiving any additional shares. Which statement is correct?
choices: Ortiz may deduct the $40,000 as a business expense
The corporation has $40,000 of gross income
The corporation excludes the contribution, and Ortiz increases the basis of her existing shares by $40,000
Ortiz must recognize gain because no stock was received
questions.exp: A shareholder's contribution to capital is excluded from the corporation's income under §118 and is added to the shareholder's basis in existing stock. Receiving no new shares does not make the contribution taxable or deductible.

questions.q: Pell Corp., a calendar-year corporation, began business on July 1 and incurred $52,000 of qualifying organizational expenditures. It elects the maximum current deduction and amortizes the rest. What is its total deduction for organizational expenditures for the first year?
questions.exp: The immediate deduction is $5,000 reduced by the $2,000 excess over $50,000, or $3,000; the remaining $49,000 is amortized over 180 months: $49,000 ÷ 180 × 6 = $1,633, for a total of $4,633. Taking the full $5,000 ignores the dollar-for-dollar phase-down.

questions.q: Which cost incurred in forming a corporation is NOT an organizational expenditure eligible for deduction and amortization under §248?
choices: Commissions paid to underwriters for selling the corporation's stock
State incorporation fees
Fees for accounting services incident to organization
Legal fees for drafting the corporate charter and bylaws
questions.exp: Costs of issuing or selling stock, such as underwriting commissions and printing stock certificates, reduce paid-in capital and are neither deductible nor amortizable. Charter, incorporation and organizational accounting and legal fees qualify under §248.

questions.q: Quinn transferred property with a fair market value of $60,000 and an adjusted basis of $90,000 to his controlled corporation. He would prefer to recognize the $30,000 loss. Which statement is correct?
choices: Quinn cannot recognize the loss, because §351 is mandatory when its requirements are met
Quinn recognizes half the loss and defers the rest
Quinn recognizes the loss because §351 applies only to gains
Quinn may elect out of §351 to recognize the loss
questions.exp: Section 351 is not elective; if the property, stock and 80% control requirements are met, both gain and loss are deferred. A taxpayer wanting the loss would need to structure a transaction that fails §351, such as a sale.

questions.q: Fay transferred land (basis $60,000, FMV $100,000) for 50 shares of a new corporation, and Gus transferred $90,000 cash and services worth $10,000 for the other 50 shares. What is Gus's basis in his shares?
questions.exp: Gus's shares count toward control because the property he contributed is not of relatively small value, so §351 applies to both transferors. Gus has $10,000 of ordinary income and a basis of $90,000 cash + $10,000 income = $100,000.

questions.q: Rios, a cash-basis sole proprietor, incorporated her business by transferring accounts receivable (basis $0, FMV $30,000) and equipment (basis $20,000) to a corporation for all its stock. The corporation assumed $35,000 of trade accounts payable that would be deductible when paid. How much gain does Rios recognize?
questions.exp: Liabilities whose payment would give rise to a deduction are excluded under §357 when testing whether liabilities exceed basis, so no gain arises even though $35,000 exceeds the $20,000 basis. Applying the excess-liability rule without the exclusion gives $15,000.

questions.q: Seth transferred property with a basis of $50,000 and a fair market value of $120,000, subject to a $30,000 liability, to his controlled corporation for stock worth $80,000 plus $10,000 cash; the corporation assumed the liability with a bona fide business purpose. What is Seth's basis in the stock?
questions.exp: Seth recognizes $10,000 gain (the cash; the liability is not boot). Stock basis = $50,000 + $10,000 gain − $10,000 cash − $30,000 liability = $20,000. Forgetting to subtract the liability gives $50,000.

questions.q: Tate transferred property with a basis of $25,000 and a fair market value of $90,000, subject to a $40,000 mortgage, to her wholly owned corporation for stock. The corporation assumed the mortgage for a bona fide business purpose. What is the corporation's basis in the property?
questions.exp: Tate recognizes $40,000 − $25,000 = $15,000 of gain under §357, and the corporation's basis is $25,000 + $15,000 = $40,000. The corporation does not take a fair market value basis.

questions.q: Which statement about §351 is correct?
choices: It can apply to transfers to an existing corporation if the transferors as a group have control immediately afterward
It applies only to the formation of a new corporation
It requires each transferor individually to own at least 80% of the stock
It applies only when transferors receive voting common stock
questions.exp: Section 351 applies to transfers to new or existing corporations; the 80% control test is applied to all transferors in the transaction as a group, and any class of stock qualifies. Individual 80% ownership is not required.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT treated as property for purposes of §351?
choices: Services rendered to the corporation
A patent or secret process
Accounts receivable of a cash-basis taxpayer
Cash
questions.exp: Section 351 excludes services from the definition of property, so stock received for services is taxable compensation and does not count toward control. Cash, receivables and intangibles are all property.

questions.q: Uma and Vic transferred property to a new corporation for 100% of its stock. Under a binding agreement made before the exchange, Uma immediately sold enough of her shares to an unrelated buyer that the transferors' combined ownership fell to 70%. What is the likely result?
choices: Section 351 applies because control existed for an instant after the exchange
The sale is ignored because it was to an unrelated buyer
Only Uma is taxed, because only she sold shares
Section 351 fails because the prearranged sale means the transferors lacked control immediately after the exchange
questions.exp: Control must exist immediately after the exchange, and a binding prearranged disposition of stock is taken into account under the step-transaction doctrine, so the transferors are treated as owning only 70%. Momentary ownership does not satisfy the test.

questions.q: Ace Corp. had $100,000 of income from operations and received $20,000 of dividends from a domestic corporation in which it owns 10% of the stock. What is Ace's dividends-received deduction?
questions.exp: A corporation owning less than 20% of the payer may deduct 50% of the dividends: 50% × $20,000 = $10,000. The taxable income limit (50% × $120,000 = $60,000) does not bind; $13,000 wrongly applies the 65% rate.

questions.q: Bay Corp. owns 30% of a domestic corporation and received $100,000 of dividends from it. Bay also had a $10,000 loss from operations, so its taxable income before the dividends-received deduction is $90,000. What is Bay's dividends-received deduction?
questions.exp: The full 65% DRD of $65,000 would not create a net operating loss ($90,000 − $65,000 = $25,000), so the deduction is limited to 65% of taxable income: 65% × $90,000 = $58,500. Taking the full $65,000 ignores the taxable income limitation.

questions.q: Cove Corp. received $200,000 of dividends from a domestic company in which it holds a 10% stake and incurred a $110,000 operating loss, leaving $90,000 of taxable income before any DRD. What dividends-received deduction may Cove claim?
questions.exp: The full 50% × $200,000 = $100,000 DRD would create a net operating loss ($90,000 − $100,000 = −$10,000), so the taxable income limitation does not apply and the full $100,000 is allowed. Limiting it to 50% × $90,000 = $45,000 overlooks the NOL exception.

questions.q: Dell Corp. owns 85% of the stock of Elm Corp., and both are members of the same affiliated group. Elm paid Dell a $200,000 dividend. What percentage of the dividend may Dell deduct as a dividends-received deduction?
questions.exp: Dividends from a member of the same affiliated group (generally 80% or more ownership) qualify for a 100% dividends-received deduction. The 65% rate applies to ownership of at least 20% but less than 80%.

questions.q: Fox Corp. bought stock of a domestic corporation five days before the ex-dividend date and sold it ten days after the ex-dividend date. What is the effect on Fox's dividends-received deduction for the dividend received?
choices: The DRD is reduced by half
No DRD is allowed because the stock was not held for more than 45 days during the required 91-day period
The DRD is allowed in full because Fox owned the stock on the record date
The DRD is allowed but treated as a tax preference
questions.exp: A corporation must hold the stock more than 45 days during the 91-day period beginning 45 days before the ex-dividend date to claim the DRD (§246). Owning the shares on the record date alone is not enough.

questions.q: Gale Corp. made $120,000 of cash contributions to qualified charities this year. Its taxable income computed without the charitable contribution deduction, the dividends-received deduction, and any NOL or capital loss carrybacks is $800,000, which includes $100,000 of dividends eligible for a $50,000 DRD. What is Gale's charitable contribution deduction for the year?
questions.exp: A corporation's charitable deduction is capped at 10% of taxable income computed before the charitable deduction and the DRD: 10% × $800,000 = $80,000. Computing the limit after subtracting the $50,000 DRD gives $75,000, which is the common error. For tax years beginning after 2025, contributions count only to the extent they exceed 1% of that same income ($8,000 here), which leaves $112,000 and does not change the $80,000 cap.

questions.q: Corporate charitable contributions that exceed the annual percentage limitation are:
choices: Carried back two years and forward 20 years
Carried forward for five years
Carried forward indefinitely
Lost permanently
questions.exp: Excess corporate charitable contributions are carried forward five years and are deductible in those years subject to the annual limitation, after current-year contributions. Indefinite carryforward applies to corporate NOLs, not contributions.

questions.q: Hart Corp. had $200,000 of income from operations, a $10,000 long-term capital gain, and a $25,000 short-term capital loss this year. What is Hart's taxable income?
questions.exp: A corporation may deduct capital losses only to the extent of capital gains, so the $15,000 net capital loss is not deductible this year and taxable income is $200,000; the excess is carried back three years and forward five. The $3,000 ordinary-income offset ($197,000) is available only to individuals.

questions.q: When a corporation carries a net capital loss back or forward to another tax year, the loss is treated as:
choices: A loss of the same character it had in the year it arose
A long-term capital loss
A short-term capital loss
An ordinary loss
questions.exp: Corporate net capital loss carrybacks and carryovers are treated as short-term capital losses in the year to which they are carried, and they offset only capital gains. Individuals, by contrast, keep the original character of their carryovers.

questions.q: Iris Corp. had current earnings and profits of $40,000 and no accumulated E&P. It distributed $60,000 cash to its sole shareholder, whose stock basis was $15,000. How much capital gain does the shareholder recognize?
questions.exp: $40,000 is a dividend from current E&P, $15,000 is a nontaxable return of capital that reduces basis to zero, and the remaining $5,000 is capital gain. Treating the entire $20,000 non-dividend portion as gain ignores recovery of basis.

questions.q: Jade Corp. had current E&P of $30,000 and an accumulated E&P deficit of $50,000 at the beginning of the year. It distributed $40,000 cash to its sole shareholder during the year. What amount is a taxable dividend?
questions.exp: Distributions are dividends to the extent of current E&P regardless of an accumulated deficit, so $30,000 is a dividend; the current and accumulated amounts are not netted when current E&P is positive. Netting them to a negative balance and concluding $0 is the classic mistake.

questions.q: Kent Corp. began the year with accumulated E&P of $20,000 and had a current E&P deficit of $24,000 for the year, which accrued ratably. On June 30 (exactly half of the year), it distributed $15,000 to its sole shareholder. What amount is a taxable dividend?
questions.exp: When current E&P is negative, the deficit is prorated to the distribution date and netted against accumulated E&P: $20,000 − ($24,000 × 1/2) = $8,000 dividend, with the rest a return of capital. Netting the full-year deficit gives $0, which is wrong for a midyear distribution.

questions.q: Lark Corp. distributed land with an adjusted basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $50,000 to its sole shareholder. Lark has ample E&P. What gain does Lark recognize, and what is the shareholder's dividend?
choices: No gain; $50,000 dividend
$30,000 gain; $20,000 dividend
No gain; $20,000 dividend
$30,000 gain; $50,000 dividend
questions.exp: A corporation recognizes gain on distributing appreciated property as if sold at fair market value (§311): $50,000 − $20,000 = $30,000. The shareholder's dividend is measured by the property's $50,000 fair market value, not the corporation's basis.

questions.q: Moss Corp., which has ample E&P, distributed land with a basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $80,000 to its sole shareholder. The land was subject to a $20,000 mortgage that the shareholder assumed. What is the shareholder's basis in the land?
questions.exp: A shareholder's basis in distributed property is its fair market value, $80,000; the liability reduces the amount of the distribution ($80,000 − $20,000 = $60,000 dividend) but not the basis. Using the $60,000 dividend amount as basis is the tempting error.

questions.q: Nile Corp. distributed equipment with an adjusted basis of $50,000 and a fair market value of $35,000 to a shareholder as a nonliquidating distribution. What loss may Nile recognize?
choices: $15,000 capital loss
$15,000, deferred until the shareholder sells the equipment
$15,000 ordinary loss
questions.exp: Under §311 a corporation recognizes gain, but not loss, on a nonliquidating distribution of property. Nile would need to sell the equipment and distribute the cash to recognize the $15,000 loss.

questions.q: In computing current earnings and profits, which item is added to taxable income?
choices: Tax-exempt municipal bond interest
Federal income taxes paid
Net capital loss in excess of capital gains
The nondeductible portion of business meals
questions.exp: Tax-exempt interest is economic income that increases E&P even though it is excluded from taxable income. Federal income taxes, excess capital losses and nondeductible meals are subtracted because they reduce the corporation's ability to pay dividends.

questions.q: Opal Corp. had taxable income of $300,000, federal income tax of $63,000, tax-exempt interest of $10,000, and a dividends-received deduction of $15,000. Ignoring other adjustments, what is Opal's current earnings and profits?
questions.exp: E&P = $300,000 + $10,000 tax-exempt interest + $15,000 DRD add-back − $63,000 federal tax = $262,000. Omitting the DRD add-back gives $247,000; the DRD is an artificial deduction that does not reduce E&P.

questions.q: Pine Corp. reported book net income of $400,000. Its records show federal income tax expense of $84,000, tax-exempt interest income of $6,000, and a $10,000 net capital loss deducted for book purposes. What is Pine's taxable income?
questions.exp: Taxable income = $400,000 + $84,000 federal tax expense + $10,000 nondeductible net capital loss − $6,000 tax-exempt interest = $488,000. Forgetting to add back the capital loss gives $478,000; corporations cannot deduct net capital losses.

questions.q: On Schedule M-1, which item is added to book income to reconcile to taxable income?
choices: Premiums paid on key-person life insurance when the corporation is the beneficiary
Tax-exempt municipal bond interest
Proceeds of a key-person life insurance policy collected by the corporation
Tax depreciation in excess of book depreciation
questions.exp: Premiums on life insurance where the corporation is the beneficiary are expensed for books but nondeductible, so they are added back. Policy proceeds and tax-exempt interest are subtracted because they are book income that is not taxable, and excess tax depreciation is also a subtraction.

questions.q: Which corporations are required to file Schedule M-3 instead of Schedule M-1 with Form 1120?
choices: Corporations with total assets of $10 million or more at the end of the year
All publicly traded corporations, regardless of size
Corporations with gross receipts of $1 million or more
Corporations that have book-tax differences exceeding 10% of book income
questions.exp: Schedule M-3 is required for corporations reporting total assets of $10 million or more on Schedule L at year-end; smaller corporations use Schedule M-1. The requirement turns on total assets, not gross receipts or public trading.

questions.q: Quay Corp. distributed a pro rata common stock dividend on its common stock; shareholders had no option to receive cash or other property. How is the distribution treated by the shareholders?
choices: It is taxable to the extent of the corporation's E&P
It is nontaxable, and shareholders allocate their existing basis between old and new shares
It is a taxable capital gain equal to the par value of the new shares
It is a taxable dividend equal to the fair market value of the new shares
questions.exp: Under §305 a pro rata stock dividend of common on common is generally excluded from income, and the shareholder's basis is allocated across old and new shares by relative value. It becomes taxable if any shareholder could elect cash or property instead.

questions.q: On audit, the IRS determines that $150,000 of the salary Reed Corp. paid to its controlling shareholder-employee was unreasonable compensation. Reed has ample E&P. What is the effect?
choices: The $150,000 is treated as a loan from Reed to the shareholder
Reed may still deduct the $150,000, and the shareholder reports it as wages
Reed loses the deduction for the $150,000, and the shareholder reports it as a dividend
Reed loses the deduction, and the shareholder excludes the $150,000 from income
questions.exp: Excess compensation to a shareholder-employee is recharacterized as a constructive dividend: nondeductible to the corporation and dividend income to the shareholder. The shareholder still has income; only its character changes.

questions.q: Sage, an individual, owned 100 shares of Tull Corp. with a basis of $30,000. Tull redeemed all of Sage's shares for $100,000, and no family attribution rules apply because no relatives own stock. Tull has ample E&P. How does Sage treat the redemption?
choices: $100,000 capital gain
$70,000 dividend
$100,000 dividend
$70,000 capital gain
questions.exp: A complete termination of the shareholder's interest under §302 is treated as a sale or exchange, so Sage recovers basis and recognizes $100,000 − $30,000 = $70,000 of capital gain. Dividend treatment applies only if the redemption fails all of the §302 exchange tests.

questions.q: Vale owned 60 of the 100 outstanding shares of Wynn Corp. (the only class), and the rest were owned by unrelated persons. Wynn redeemed 30 of Vale's shares. Does the redemption qualify as substantially disproportionate under §302?
choices: No, because Vale's ownership fell by only half
Yes, because Vale's ownership fell below 50% of the shares outstanding before the redemption
Yes, because Vale now owns 30 ÷ 70 = 42.9%, which is less than 50% and less than 80% of her former 60%
No, because Vale still owns stock after the redemption
questions.exp: After the redemption Vale owns 30 of 70 shares, or 42.9%, which is below 50% and below 80% × 60% = 48%, so the redemption is substantially disproportionate and gets exchange treatment. The test uses shares outstanding after the redemption, not before.

questions.q: Xeno Corp. has a $500,000 net operating loss carryforward that arose in 2023. Its 2026 taxable income before the NOL deduction is $400,000. What is Xeno's NOL deduction for 2026?
questions.exp: NOLs arising after 2017 may offset only 80% of taxable income: 80% × $400,000 = $320,000, and the remaining $180,000 carries forward indefinitely. Deducting $400,000 applies the pre-2018 rule that allowed a full offset.

questions.q: Yard Corp., an accrual-basis calendar-year corporation, accrued a $50,000 bonus on December 31, Year 1, to its president, a cash-basis taxpayer who owns 60% of Yard's stock. The bonus was paid on February 15, Year 2. When may Yard deduct the bonus?
choices: Never, because it is a payment to a majority shareholder
Year 1, because it was paid within two and one-half months after year-end
Year 2, when the president includes the payment in income
Year 1, because all events fixing the liability occurred in Year 1
questions.exp: Under §267, an accrual-basis payer may not deduct an amount owed to a related cash-basis payee (an individual owning more than 50% of the stock) until the payee includes it in income, so the deduction is in Year 2. The 2½-month rule applies only to unrelated employees.

questions.q: Zane Corp. had a $100,000 net long-term capital gain and $500,000 of ordinary taxable income. How is the capital gain taxed?
choices: At the regular 21% corporate rate
At a maximum rate of 20%
At a maximum rate of 15%
At 21% only to the extent of capital losses carried forward
questions.exp: Corporations do not receive a preferential rate on net capital gains; all taxable income, including capital gains, is taxed at the flat 21% rate. The 15% and 20% rates apply to individuals.

questions.q: During the year Able Corp. paid $10,000 for client entertainment (a sporting event), $8,000 for business meals with clients at which business was discussed, and a $5,000 fine to a state agency for a regulatory violation. How much of these costs may Able deduct?
questions.exp: Entertainment expenses are nondeductible, fines paid to a government are nondeductible, and business meals are 50% deductible: 50% × $8,000 = $4,000. Applying 50% to both entertainment and meals gives $9,000, which reflects pre-2018 law.

questions.q: Brant Corp. had accumulated E&P of $100,000 before it distributed land with a basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $50,000 to its shareholder. Ignoring income taxes, what is Brant's E&P after the distribution?
questions.exp: E&P increases by the $30,000 gain recognized and then decreases by the $50,000 fair market value of the appreciated property distributed: $100,000 + $30,000 − $50,000 = $80,000. Subtracting $50,000 without first adding the recognized gain gives $50,000.

questions.q: Which statement about the accumulated earnings tax is correct?
choices: It is self-assessed on Form 1120 by every corporation with accumulated E&P
It is imposed on a corporation's total accumulated E&P regardless of business needs
It applies to S corporations that were formerly C corporations
It is imposed on earnings accumulated beyond the reasonable needs of the business to avoid shareholder-level tax on dividends
questions.exp: The accumulated earnings tax is a penalty tax on accumulated taxable income retained beyond reasonable business needs for the purpose of avoiding shareholder income tax, and it is assessed by the IRS rather than self-reported. Corporations may retain earnings up to reasonable needs and the statutory credit without penalty.

questions.q: Dex Corp. has 20 creditors and is not paying its debts as they become due. Assume the Bankruptcy Code requires petitioning creditors' qualifying claims to total at least $20,000 in the aggregate. Which group of creditors may file an involuntary Chapter 7 petition against Dex?
choices: Three creditors with claims of $8,000, $7,000 and $6,000 that are fully secured by collateral
Two creditors with unsecured, undisputed claims totaling $50,000
Three creditors whose claims totaling $30,000 are subject to a bona fide dispute as to liability
Three creditors with unsecured, undisputed claims of $8,000, $7,000 and $6,000
questions.exp: When a debtor has 12 or more creditors, at least three creditors holding noncontingent, undisputed claims whose unsecured portions total at least the threshold must join (11 U.S.C. §303). Two creditors are insufficient regardless of amount, and disputed or fully secured claims do not count.

questions.q: Creditors properly filed an involuntary Chapter 7 petition against Ewing, an individual, who contested it. On which basis will the court most likely enter an order for relief?
choices: Ewing is generally not paying his undisputed debts as they become due
Ewing failed to pay one creditor on time
Ewing's liabilities exceed the fair value of his assets on a balance-sheet basis
Ewing transferred property to a relative five years ago
questions.exp: Under §303, an order for relief on a contested involuntary petition requires that the debtor is generally not paying undisputed debts as they come due, or that a custodian took possession of substantially all property within 120 days. Balance-sheet insolvency alone is not the test.

questions.q: Against which of the following may creditors file an involuntary Chapter 7 petition?
choices: A charitable nonprofit corporation
A for-profit retail corporation that is generally not paying its debts as they become due
An insurance company
A family farmer
questions.exp: Section 303 bars involuntary petitions against farmers, family farmers and nonprofit (non-moneyed) corporations, and insurance companies and banks cannot be Chapter 7 debtors at all. Ordinary business corporations may be involuntary debtors.

questions.q: Fay filed a voluntary Chapter 7 petition. Which action may proceed despite the automatic stay?
choices: A landlord's letter demanding past-due rent
A secured creditor's repossession of Fay's car
A creditor's lawsuit to collect a pre-petition credit card debt
A proceeding to collect a domestic support obligation from property that is not property of the estate
questions.exp: The automatic stay of §362 halts most collection activity, including suits, repossessions and demand letters, but has exceptions for criminal proceedings and for establishing or collecting domestic support obligations from non-estate property. A secured creditor must seek relief from the stay.

questions.q: Sixty days before filing a Chapter 7 petition, while insolvent, Gale paid $10,000 to an unrelated unsecured supplier on an invoice that had been past due for five months. The payment was not in the ordinary course of business. Which statement is correct?
choices: The payment is not avoidable because it was made more than 30 days before the petition
The payment is not avoidable because the supplier is not an insider
The payment is avoidable only if the supplier knew Gale was insolvent
The trustee may avoid the payment as a preference
questions.exp: Under §547, a transfer to a creditor on an antecedent debt, made while insolvent within 90 days before the petition, that gives the creditor more than it would receive in Chapter 7 is avoidable. The creditor's knowledge of insolvency is irrelevant; insider status extends the period to one year.

questions.q: Eight months before filing a Chapter 7 petition, while insolvent, Hale repaid a $15,000 unsecured loan to his brother that had been due for a year. Which statement is correct?
choices: The trustee may avoid the payment as a preference to an insider
The payment is not avoidable because it repaid a legitimate debt
The payment is avoidable only as a fraudulent transfer
The payment is not avoidable because it was made more than 90 days before the petition
questions.exp: For insiders such as relatives, the preference look-back period is one year rather than 90 days (§547). Repaying a legitimate debt is exactly what makes a transfer a preference.

questions.q: Within 90 days before filing a Chapter 7 petition, while insolvent, Ivy Corp. made the following payments. Which is most likely NOT avoidable as a preference?
choices: Payment of its monthly utility bill, made according to ordinary business terms in the ordinary course
A payment to its president on an old unsecured loan
A payment to an unsecured lender on a loan that was six months overdue
A payment to an unsecured trade creditor accelerated because the creditor threatened suit
questions.exp: Section 547 excepts payments made in the ordinary course of business according to ordinary business terms, as well as contemporaneous exchanges for new value. Late, pressured or insider payments on old debts are classic preferences.

questions.q: Eighteen months before filing for bankruptcy, while insolvent, Jay transferred his vacation home worth $300,000 to his cousin for $20,000. Which statement is correct?
choices: The transfer cannot be avoided because the cousin paid some consideration
The trustee may avoid the transfer as a fraudulent conveyance because it was made within two years for less than reasonably equivalent value while insolvent
The transfer cannot be avoided because it occurred more than one year before the petition
The transfer is a preference avoidable only if the cousin is an insider
questions.exp: Under §548, a transfer within two years before the petition for less than reasonably equivalent value while insolvent is constructively fraudulent and avoidable, without proof of intent. It is not a preference because the cousin was not a creditor.

questions.q: In a Chapter 7 liquidation, which of the following unsecured claims is entitled to the highest priority?
choices: Wages owed to the debtor's employees
General unsecured trade claims
A domestic support obligation owed to the debtor's former spouse
Federal income taxes owed by the debtor
questions.exp: Under §507, domestic support obligations are first-priority unsecured claims (subject to trustee administrative costs related to them), ahead of wages and taxes. General unsecured claims share only after all priority claims are paid.

questions.q: An employee is owed $18,000 of wages earned within 180 days before her employer's Chapter 7 petition. Assume the per-employee wage priority cap is $15,000. How is her claim treated?
choices: $18,000 as a general unsecured claim
$18,000 as a priority claim
$15,000 as a priority claim; the remaining $3,000 is discharged without payment
$15,000 as a priority claim and $3,000 as a general unsecured claim
questions.exp: Wage claims earned within 180 days are priority claims under §507 only up to the statutory cap; the excess is a general unsecured claim that shares pro rata with other unsecured creditors. The excess is not simply disallowed.

questions.q: Kirk Bank holds a $55,000 claim against a Chapter 7 debtor secured by equipment worth $40,000. The estate will pay general unsecured creditors 20% of their claims. How much will Kirk Bank receive in total?
questions.exp: Under §506, an undersecured claim is bifurcated: $40,000 is secured and paid from the collateral, and the $15,000 deficiency is a general unsecured claim receiving 20%, or $3,000, for $43,000. Treating the entire claim as secured gives $55,000.

questions.q: Which of the following debts of an individual would ordinarily be discharged in a Chapter 7 bankruptcy?
choices: A student loan, absent a showing of undue hardship
A judgment for injuries the debtor caused while driving intoxicated
Past-due child support
Credit card charges for groceries incurred without fraud a year before filing
questions.exp: Section 523 excepts from discharge domestic support obligations, most student loans (absent undue hardship) and debts for personal injury caused by intoxicated driving, among others. Ordinary consumer debts incurred without fraud are dischargeable.

questions.q: Which of the following would cause a court to deny an individual Chapter 7 debtor a discharge of all debts?
choices: The debtor concealed valuable property from the trustee with intent to defraud creditors
The debtor's debts are primarily business debts
The debtor received a Chapter 7 discharge ten years ago
The debtor owes nondischargeable student loans
questions.exp: Under §727, a discharge is denied entirely for acts such as concealing property with intent to defraud, making a false oath, or having received a Chapter 7 discharge in a case filed within eight years. Nondischargeable debts are excepted individually without denying the whole discharge.

questions.q: Lark Corp. filed a voluntary Chapter 7 petition and its assets were liquidated and distributed. Which statement is correct?
choices: Lark Corp. does not receive a discharge in Chapter 7
Lark Corp. may keep exempt property up to the state limit
Lark Corp. may claim the federal homestead exemption
Lark Corp. receives a discharge of its remaining unpaid debts
questions.exp: Under §727, only individuals receive a Chapter 7 discharge; a liquidated corporation simply ceases operating with debts undischarged. Exemptions likewise apply only to individual debtors.

questions.q: Mona, a Chapter 7 debtor not represented by an attorney, wants to keep her car by reaffirming the loan with her lender. Which statement is correct?
choices: A reaffirmation agreement cannot be rescinded once signed
A reaffirmation agreement may be oral
The agreement must be made before discharge and filed with the court, and Mona may rescind it before the later of discharge or 60 days after filing
A reaffirmation agreement may be made at any time after the discharge
questions.exp: Section 524 requires a reaffirmation agreement to be made before discharge and filed with the court, gives the debtor a right to rescind until the later of discharge or 60 days after filing, and requires court approval for unrepresented debtors. Agreements after discharge are unenforceable.

questions.q: Nate, an individual with primarily consumer debts, filed a Chapter 7 petition. His current monthly income exceeds the median family income for his state, and after allowed expenses he has substantial disposable income. Which statement is correct?
choices: Nate's case will automatically be converted to Chapter 11
The means test applies only to business debts
Nate's case must be dismissed because Chapter 7 is unavailable to individuals with above-median income
A presumption of abuse arises, and the case may be dismissed or, with Nate's consent, converted to Chapter 13
questions.exp: Under the §707 means test, an above-median debtor with primarily consumer debts and sufficient disposable income faces a presumption of abuse, which can lead to dismissal or conversion to Chapter 13 with consent. The presumption can be rebutted by special circumstances.

questions.q: In a Chapter 11 reorganization, a class of unsecured creditors has 100 members holding $1,000,000 of allowed claims. Sixty members holding $600,000 of claims voted. Of those voting, 40 members holding $420,000 voted to accept the plan. Has the class accepted the plan?
choices: Yes, because more than one-half in number and at least two-thirds in amount of those voting accepted
No, because less than one-half of all class members accepted
No, because less than two-thirds of the total claims in the class accepted
Yes, because a majority of the total dollar amount voting accepted
questions.exp: Under §1126, a class accepts if creditors holding at least two-thirds in amount and more than one-half in number of the allowed claims actually voting accept: 40/60 = 67% in number and $420,000/$600,000 = 70% in amount. Measuring against all class members, rather than those voting, is the trap.

questions.q: Which of the following may file for relief under Chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code?
choices: A partnership with regular income
An individual with no source of income
A corporation with regular income
An individual with regular income whose debts are within the Chapter 13 debt limits
questions.exp: Chapter 13 is available only to individuals (including sole proprietors) with regular income whose debts are within statutory limits (§109). Corporations and partnerships must use Chapter 11 to reorganize.

questions.q: Before filing for bankruptcy, Ola Co. granted Pine Bank a security interest in its equipment. Pine Bank never filed a financing statement or otherwise perfected. What can the bankruptcy trustee do?
choices: Avoid the security interest only if Pine Bank is an insider
Avoid the security interest using the trustee's status as a hypothetical lien creditor
Nothing, because the security interest attached before the petition
Avoid the security interest only if it was granted within 90 days
questions.exp: Under the strong-arm clause of §544, the trustee has the rights of a hypothetical lien creditor as of the petition date, and an unperfected security interest is subordinate to a lien creditor. Pine Bank becomes a general unsecured creditor.

questions.q: Rae filed a Chapter 7 petition on January 15. Which of the following is property of the bankruptcy estate?
choices: Wages Rae earns for work performed after January 15
A gift of cash Rae receives from a friend on June 1
An inheritance Rae becomes entitled to on May 1 from her aunt's death on that date
Property Rae buys with post-petition wages
questions.exp: The estate includes property the debtor owns at filing plus property acquired by inheritance, divorce settlement or life insurance within 180 days after filing (§541). Post-petition earnings of an individual in Chapter 7 and ordinary post-petition gifts are excluded.

questions.q: Within 90 days before filing a Chapter 7 petition, while insolvent, Sky Co. made a $20,000 payment to Trust Bank on a past-due loan. Trust Bank held a perfected security interest in Sky's equipment worth $50,000, and the loan balance before the payment was $40,000. Is the payment avoidable as a preference?
choices: Yes, because it was paid on an antecedent debt within 90 days
Yes, because Sky was insolvent when it paid
No, because Trust Bank is an insider
No, because Trust Bank was fully secured and did not receive more than it would have in a Chapter 7 liquidation
questions.exp: A preference requires that the creditor receive more than it would in a Chapter 7 liquidation (§547); a fully secured creditor would be paid in full from its collateral anyway. Antecedent debt and insolvency alone are not enough.

questions.q: Uma guaranteed Vic's $30,000 loan from Wes Bank as a surety. Vic defaulted, and Uma paid the bank in full. The bank had held a security interest in Vic's truck. What rights does Uma have?
choices: Only a right to sue the bank for failing to collect from Vic first
A right of reimbursement from Vic and subrogation to the bank's rights, including its security interest in the truck
Only a right of contribution against Vic
No rights, because she voluntarily guaranteed the loan
questions.exp: A surety who pays the debt has a right of reimbursement from the principal debtor and is subrogated to the creditor's rights against the debtor, including collateral. Contribution runs between co-sureties, not against the debtor.

questions.q: Xena was a compensated surety on Yale's $50,000 loan. Without Xena's consent, the lender released its security interest in Yale's equipment, worth $20,000. Yale then defaulted. What is the effect on Xena's liability?
choices: Xena's liability is unaffected
Xena is fully discharged
Xena is liable for the full $50,000 but may sue the lender for negligence
Xena is discharged to the extent of the $20,000 value of the released collateral
questions.exp: A creditor's release or impairment of collateral discharges the surety to the extent of the value of the collateral released, because it impairs the surety's subrogation rights. A release of collateral does not discharge the surety entirely.

questions.q: Kyle and Lena are co-sureties on Mo's $60,000 debt. Kyle guaranteed up to $50,000 and Lena up to $100,000. Mo defaulted, and Lena paid the creditor the entire $60,000. How much can Lena recover from Kyle by way of contribution?
questions.exp: Co-sureties share in proportion to the amounts they guaranteed: Kyle's share is $50,000 / $150,000 × $60,000 = $20,000. An equal split would give $30,000, which ignores the different limits.

questions.q: Zoe signed as a surety for Ned's loan. Ned defaulted, and the creditor sued Zoe. Which of the following is NOT a defense available to Zoe?
choices: Ned's incapacity because he was a minor when he borrowed
A material modification of Ned's loan made without Zoe's consent
The creditor's prior acceptance of full payment from Ned
Fraud by the creditor that induced Zoe to sign
questions.exp: A surety cannot use defenses personal to the debtor, such as the debtor's minority, insolvency or bankruptcy; protecting against those risks is often the reason for the guarantee. Creditor fraud on the surety, material modification and payment are surety defenses.

questions.q: A judgment creditor seeks to garnish the wages of a debtor whose disposable earnings are $800 per week. The debt is an ordinary consumer debt, not support, taxes or bankruptcy-related. Assume the minimum-wage-based floor does not limit the garnishment. Under federal law, what is the maximum amount that may be garnished each week?
questions.exp: The Consumer Credit Protection Act generally limits garnishment for ordinary debts to 25% of disposable earnings (or the excess over 30 times the minimum wage, if less): 25% × $800 = $200. Higher limits apply to support orders.

questions.q: Opie, who is in financial difficulty, entered into a composition agreement with four of his six creditors, each agreeing to accept 60% of its claim in full satisfaction. Which statement is correct?
choices: The agreement is unenforceable for lack of consideration
The agreement binds all six creditors
The agreement automatically places Opie in bankruptcy
The agreement binds only the four creditors who agreed; the other two may pursue their full claims
questions.exp: A common law composition is a contract among the debtor and participating creditors; the creditors' mutual promises supply consideration, but nonparticipating creditors are not bound. Only a bankruptcy plan can bind dissenters.

questions.q: Pia, an individual, wants to file a voluntary Chapter 7 petition. Which statement is correct?
choices: She must obtain the consent of a majority of her creditors
She must have at least 12 creditors
She must prove she is insolvent
She need not be insolvent, but generally must receive credit counseling from an approved agency within 180 days before filing
questions.exp: A voluntary petition does not require insolvency or any minimum number of creditors, but under §109 an individual debtor generally must receive approved credit counseling within 180 days before filing. Creditor consent is irrelevant to a voluntary case.

questions.q: Lender A recorded a mortgage on Quill's land in Year 1. In Year 3, Judgment Creditor B obtained and properly recorded a judgment lien against the land. Quill defaulted on both, and the land was sold for less than the total owed. Outside bankruptcy, which party has priority in the proceeds?
choices: Judgment Creditor B, because its lien arose more recently
Lender A and Judgment Creditor B share pro rata
Judgment Creditor B, because judgment liens take priority over consensual liens
Lender A, because its mortgage was recorded first
questions.exp: Under state recording law, liens on real property generally rank in order of recording, so the earlier recorded mortgage has priority over a later judgment lien. Judicial liens receive no special priority over prior perfected interests.

questions.q: After secured creditors were paid from their collateral, a Chapter 7 estate has $100,000 of cash. Administrative expenses are $10,000, priority tax claims are $30,000, and general unsecured claims total $120,000. Rex holds a $24,000 general unsecured claim. How much will Rex receive?
questions.exp: Priority claims are paid first ($10,000 + $30,000), leaving $60,000 for $120,000 of general unsecured claims, a 50% dividend; Rex receives 50% × $24,000 = $12,000 (§§507, 726). Sharing the full $100,000 pro rata ignores the priorities and gives $20,000.

questions.q: During the current year Carl, who is married, gave $50,000 cash to his son. Carl's wife made no gifts. Carl and his wife elected gift splitting. Assume the gift tax annual exclusion is $19,000 per donee. What is the amount of Carl's taxable gift?
questions.exp: With gift splitting (§2513), each spouse is treated as giving $25,000; after a $19,000 exclusion each has a $6,000 taxable gift. Ignoring the election gives Carl alone a $31,000 taxable gift.

questions.q: Dana transferred $100,000 to an irrevocable trust. The trustee may accumulate income or distribute it to Dana's niece at the trustee's discretion until the niece reaches age 30, when the trust terminates and the niece receives all the property. The niece has no withdrawal rights. Assume the annual exclusion is $19,000. What is Dana's taxable gift?
questions.exp: The annual exclusion applies only to gifts of present interests (§2503); the niece's rights are future interests because distributions are discretionary and deferred, so the full $100,000 is a taxable gift. Subtracting the exclusion is the common mistake.

questions.q: This year Gwen paid $60,000 of tuition directly to a university on behalf of her grandson and gave him $25,000 cash for books and living expenses. She made no other gifts to him. Assume the annual exclusion is $19,000. What is Gwen's taxable gift to her grandson?
questions.exp: Tuition paid directly to an educational organization is an unlimited exclusion under §2503 (separate from the annual exclusion), so only $25,000 − $19,000 = $6,000 is taxable. Books and living expenses do not qualify for the tuition exclusion.

questions.q: During the year Henry gave stock worth $500,000 to his wife, a U.S. citizen, and gave $500,000 cash to a qualified public charity. Assume the annual exclusion is $19,000. What is the total of Henry's taxable gifts for the year?
questions.exp: Gifts to a U.S.-citizen spouse qualify for the unlimited marital deduction (§2523) and gifts to charity for the unlimited charitable deduction (§2522), so taxable gifts are $0. Allowing only the annual exclusions is the trap.

questions.q: Which of the following is included in a decedent's gross estate?
choices: Proceeds of a policy on the decedent's life purchased and always owned by her son
A remainder interest in a trust created by the decedent's father that terminated at the decedent's death
Proceeds of a policy on the decedent's life payable to her son, where the decedent retained the right to change the beneficiary
Cash the decedent gave to her daughter five years before death, on which no gift tax was paid
questions.exp: Life insurance is included under §2042 if the decedent held any incident of ownership, such as the right to change beneficiaries, regardless of who is the beneficiary. Lifetime gifts are added back only as adjusted taxable gifts, not as gross estate items.

questions.q: At death, Ian and his wife owned real estate as joint tenants with right of survivorship. The property was worth $800,000 at Ian's death, and Ian had furnished all of the purchase price. How much is included in Ian's gross estate?
questions.exp: For joint interests held only by spouses, one-half is included regardless of who furnished consideration (§2040). The consideration-furnished test applies only to joint tenancies with non-spouses.

questions.q: Jill and her brother owned land as joint tenants with right of survivorship. Jill furnished 75% of the purchase price and her brother furnished 25%. The land was worth $600,000 at Jill's death. How much is included in Jill's gross estate?
questions.exp: For joint tenancies with non-spouses, the decedent's gross estate includes the property's value except the portion attributable to the survivor's contribution (§2040): 75% × $600,000 = $450,000. The automatic one-half rule applies only to spouses.

questions.q: Two years before her death, Kim made a taxable gift of stock to her nephew and paid $40,000 of gift tax. The stock appreciated significantly before her death. Which amount relating to this gift is included in Kim's gross estate?
choices: The fair market value of the stock at Kim's death
The stock's value at the gift date plus the $40,000 gift tax
The fair market value of the stock on the date of the gift
Only the $40,000 of gift tax paid
questions.exp: Under §2035, gift tax paid on gifts within three years of death is grossed up into the gross estate; the gifted stock itself is not included but is added to the tax base as an adjusted taxable gift. Including the stock at death value confuses this with retained-interest transfers.

questions.q: At Lou's death his estate held stock worth $1,000,000. The executor sold the stock four months after death for $950,000. Six months after death, the same stock would have been worth $900,000. If the executor validly elects the alternate valuation date, at what value is the stock included in the gross estate?
questions.exp: Under §2032, property sold or distributed within six months after death is valued on the date of disposition, here $950,000. The six-month value applies only to property still held at that date.

questions.q: Which statement about the estate tax alternate valuation election is correct?
choices: It may be elected by any estate required to file, even if no estate tax is due
It values property one year after the date of death
It may be elected only if it decreases both the gross estate and the sum of the estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax
It may be elected on a property-by-property basis
questions.exp: Section 2032 requires that the election reduce both the gross estate value and the estate (and GST) tax, and it applies to all estate property. Because it must reduce tax, it cannot be used merely to step up basis in a nontaxable estate.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT deductible in computing a decedent's taxable estate?
choices: Federal income tax on income earned by the estate after the date of death
Reasonable funeral expenses
A mortgage on residential property included in the gross estate at its full value
Unpaid federal income tax on income the decedent earned before death
questions.exp: Debts of the decedent, including income tax on pre-death income, are deductible under §2053, but income tax on the estate's post-death income is an obligation of the estate, not of the decedent. Funeral expenses and mortgages on included property are deductible.

questions.q: Mae's gross estate is $16,000,000. Funeral and administration expenses total $200,000, she bequeathed $4,000,000 to her husband (a U.S. citizen) outright, and $800,000 to a qualified charity. What is Mae's taxable estate?
questions.exp: $16,000,000 − $200,000 expenses − $4,000,000 marital deduction − $800,000 charitable deduction = $11,000,000 (§§2053, 2055, 2056). Omitting the unlimited charitable deduction gives $11,800,000.

questions.q: Ned's taxable estate is $9,000,000. Ten years before death, Ned made gifts that, after annual exclusions, resulted in $2,000,000 of taxable gifts. He also made gifts totaling $200,000 that were fully covered by annual exclusions. What amount is used as the base for computing Ned's tentative estate tax?
questions.exp: The tentative tax base is the taxable estate plus post-1976 adjusted taxable gifts (§2001): $9,000,000 + $2,000,000 = $11,000,000. Gifts sheltered by the annual exclusion are never taxable gifts and are not added back.

questions.q: Omar died this year, having used $4,000,000 of his basic exclusion amount. His wife, Pam, survives him. Assume the basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 for both. What exclusion amount will be available to Pam for her later lifetime gifts or estate, assuming she does not remarry?
choices: $15,000,000, because unused exclusion cannot be transferred between spouses
$26,000,000 automatically, with no election required
$26,000,000, provided Omar's executor elected portability on a timely filed estate tax return
questions.exp: The deceased spousal unused exclusion (DSUE) of $11,000,000 is added to Pam's own $15,000,000 only if Omar's executor makes the portability election on a timely filed Form 706 (§2010). Portability is not automatic.

questions.q: Quinn inherited stock from her father, who had purchased it for $20,000. The stock was worth $90,000 at the father's death, and the alternate valuation date was not elected. Two months after the death, Quinn sold the stock for $95,000. What gain does Quinn recognize?
choices: $5,000 long-term capital gain
$75,000 long-term capital gain
$5,000 short-term capital gain
questions.exp: Inherited property takes a basis equal to FMV at death under §1014 ($90,000), and its holding period is automatically long-term under §1223, so the gain is $5,000 long-term. The donor's $20,000 carryover basis applies to gifts, not bequests.

questions.q: Ruth received stock as a gift. The donor's basis was $40,000 and the fair market value at the date of the gift was $30,000. No gift tax was paid. Ruth later sold the stock for $35,000. What gain or loss does Ruth recognize?
choices: $5,000 gain
$5,000 loss
No gain or loss
questions.exp: Under §1015 dual-basis rules, the gain basis is $40,000 (no gain) and the loss basis is the $30,000 FMV (no loss), so a sale between the two produces no gain or loss. Using the donor's basis for a loss is the common error.

questions.q: Which statement about the federal gift tax return (Form 709) is correct?
choices: The donee is primarily liable for the tax and files the return
A return is required only if gift tax is actually due after applying the unified credit
The return is due nine months after the date of the gift
The donor is primarily liable for the tax; the return is generally due April 15 of the year following the gift, and an extension of the donor's income tax return also extends it
questions.exp: Under §§6019 and 6075 the donor files and pays, generally by April 15 of the following year, and an income tax extension extends the gift return. A return is required for taxable gifts even if the unified credit eliminates the tax.

questions.q: Sam transferred securities to a revocable trust, retaining the right to revoke it. The trust income is payable to his daughter. When does Sam make a completed gift?
choices: When the securities are transferred to the trust
When income is paid to the daughter or when Sam relinquishes the power to revoke
Never, because transfers to any trust are disregarded for gift tax purposes
Only at Sam's death
questions.exp: A transfer is a completed gift only when the donor has given up dominion and control; with a revocable trust, gifts occur as distributions are made to beneficiaries or when the power to revoke is released (Reg. §25.2511-2). Funding a revocable trust alone is incomplete.

questions.q: Tia deposited $100,000 of her own funds into a bank account held jointly with her son, who may withdraw any amount. The next year the son withdrew $30,000 for his own use. What gift has Tia made?
choices: No gift, because the account is held jointly
$100,000 at the time of deposit
$50,000 at the time of deposit
$30,000 when the son withdrew the funds
questions.exp: Because Tia can withdraw the entire deposit, there is no completed gift until the son withdraws funds for his own benefit (Reg. §25.2511-1). Treating a revocable joint bank account like a joint tenancy in real property is the trap.

questions.q: Which of the following is a requirement for a qualified disclaimer of an inheritance so that the disclaimant is not treated as making a gift?
choices: The disclaimant may first accept income from the property if it is repaid
The disclaimant may direct to whom the disclaimed property passes
The disclaimer must be made within 15 months of the decedent's death
The disclaimer must be an irrevocable written refusal made within nine months and before accepting any benefits, with the property passing without direction by the disclaimant
questions.exp: Section 2518 requires a written, irrevocable refusal delivered within nine months (or by age 21), no acceptance of benefits, and passage of the property without direction by the disclaimant. Directing the property makes it a taxable gift.

questions.q: Which bequest qualifies for the estate tax marital deduction?
choices: A life estate for the surviving spouse that terminates if the spouse remarries
A trust paying all income to the surviving spouse at least annually for life, with remainder to the decedent's children, for which the executor makes a QTIP election
A trust under which the trustee may distribute income to the decedent's children during the surviving spouse's life
An outright bequest to a surviving spouse who is a nonresident non-citizen, not through a qualified domestic trust
questions.exp: A QTIP trust satisfies §2056 because the spouse receives all income at least annually and no one else can receive property during her life. Interests terminating on remarriage or allowing distributions to others are nondeductible terminable interests.

questions.q: Uma's gross estate is $10,000,000. Her will leaves $3,000,000 to a qualified public charity. What estate tax charitable deduction is allowed?
choices: $0, because charitable deductions are allowed only for income tax
$1,000,000, limited to 10% of the gross estate
Limited to 60% of the adjusted gross estate
questions.exp: The estate tax charitable deduction under §2055 is unlimited for bequests to qualified charities. Percentage-of-income limits apply only to the income tax charitable deduction.

questions.q: Vic died on March 10 of the current year. His gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds the filing threshold. When is the federal estate tax return due, and what extension is available?
choices: April 15 of the following year, with a six-month extension
December 31 of the year of death, with no extension
December 10 of the year of death, with an automatic six-month extension available upon request
Fifteen months after death, with no extension
questions.exp: Form 706 is due nine months after the date of death (§6075), here December 10, and a six-month extension of time to file may be obtained. April 15 is the income tax and gift tax deadline.

questions.q: Twelve years before his death, Will deeded his residence to his son but retained the right to live in it rent-free for the rest of his life, and he did so. What amount relating to the residence is included in Will's gross estate?
choices: Only the value of Will's life estate
Nothing, because the transfer occurred more than three years before death
The value at the date of transfer, added only as an adjusted taxable gift
The full fair market value of the residence at Will's death
questions.exp: Under §2036, property transferred with a retained life estate (possession or enjoyment) is included at its full date-of-death value, regardless of when the transfer occurred. The three-year rule is irrelevant to retained interests.

questions.q: Xena gave 1,000 shares of a publicly traded stock to her nephew. On the date of the gift, the stock's high price was $52, its low price was $48, and its closing price was $49. What is the value of the gift for gift tax purposes, before any exclusion?
questions.exp: Listed securities are valued at the mean of the high and low selling prices on the valuation date (Reg. §25.2512-2): ($52 + $48) / 2 = $50 × 1,000 shares = $50,000. The closing price is not the valuation standard.

questions.q: Which of the following transfers is a direct skip for generation-skipping transfer tax purposes?
choices: A gift to the donor's niece
A gift to a grandchild whose parent, the donor's child, is living
A gift to an unrelated individual who is 30 years younger than the donor
A gift to a grandchild whose parent, the donor's child, died before the gift
questions.exp: A direct skip is a transfer to a skip person two or more generations below the transferor (§2612); a grandchild with a living parent qualifies. The predeceased-parent rule moves the grandchild up a generation, and a niece or unrelated person 30 years younger is only one generation below.

questions.q: Which statement about gift splitting between spouses is correct?
choices: Spouses may choose to split some gifts to third parties and not others in the same year
Spouses may split gifts made to each other
Both spouses must consent, and the election applies to all gifts made by either spouse to third parties during the calendar year
Only the donor spouse must consent
questions.exp: Under §2513, both spouses must consent, and the election covers all gifts to third parties by either spouse during that year. Gifts between spouses are covered by the marital deduction, not splitting.

questions.q: Two years before her death, Ava transferred ownership of a $1,000,000 policy on her own life to her daughter. The daughter paid all premiums after the transfer and was the beneficiary. What amount is included in Ava's gross estate?
choices: The premiums paid by the daughter
$0, because the daughter owned the policy at Ava's death
The policy's cash surrender value at the date of transfer
questions.exp: Section 2035 includes life insurance proceeds if the insured transferred incidents of ownership within three years of death. The three-year rule is one of the few remaining situations where gifted property itself is pulled back in.

questions.q: At his death, Ben was owed $30,000 of earned but unpaid salary, which his estate later collected. Which statement about this item is correct?
choices: It is included in the gross estate, does not receive a stepped-up basis, and is taxable income to the estate when collected, with an income tax deduction for estate tax attributable to it
It is reported only on Ben's final individual income tax return
It is included in the gross estate and receives a stepped-up basis, so it is not taxable income when collected
It is excluded from the gross estate because it is taxed as income
questions.exp: Income in respect of a decedent is included in the gross estate, is denied a §1014 basis step-up, and is income to the recipient under §691, which allows a deduction for the related estate tax. A cash-basis decedent never reported the salary, so it is not on the final return.

questions.q: Assume the gift tax annual exclusion is $19,000 per donee. Which of the following transfers made by Cy during the year results in a taxable gift?
choices: A $70,000 payment made directly to a hospital for a friend's surgery
A $50,000 cash transfer to his adult daughter to buy a car
A $40,000 contribution to a political organization
$30,000 of food and housing provided for his minor child, as required by state law
questions.exp: The cash to the daughter exceeds the annual exclusion by $31,000, a taxable gift. Political contributions (§2501), direct medical payments (§2503) and legally required support are not taxable gifts.

topics.topic: Filing status, dependents and tax computation

questions.q: Joan's husband died in Year 1. She has not remarried, and her 8-year-old son, whom she claims as a dependent, has lived with her in the home she maintains every year since. What is the most advantageous filing status available to Joan for Year 3?
choices: Single
Head of household
Married filing jointly
Qualifying surviving spouse
questions.exp: A surviving spouse who maintains a home for a dependent child may use qualifying surviving spouse status (joint-return rates) for the two years after the year of death, which are Years 2 and 3. Head of household is available only after that period ends.

questions.q: Kay is unmarried and has no children. Her widowed mother lives in a nursing home, and Kay pays more than half the cost of the nursing home and of her mother's support. Her mother has no gross income. What is Kay's most advantageous filing status?
choices: Single
Head of household
Qualifying surviving spouse
Married filing separately
questions.exp: A dependent parent is a qualifying person for head of household even if the parent does not live with the taxpayer, provided the taxpayer pays more than half the cost of the parent's home (including a nursing home). The usual requirement that the qualifying person live with the taxpayer does not apply to a parent.

questions.q: Lana's divorce became final on December 31 of the current year. She has no children or other dependents. What is her filing status for the current year?
choices: Head of household
Married filing separately
Married filing jointly
Single
questions.exp: Marital status is determined on the last day of the tax year, so a taxpayer divorced on December 31 is unmarried for the entire year and, without a qualifying person, files as single. Married statuses are unavailable once the final decree is entered.

questions.q: Mona is still legally married, but her husband moved out in March and has not lived in the home since. Mona paid all the costs of the home, where her 10-year-old daughter, her dependent, lived with her all year. Her husband refuses to file a joint return. What is Mona's most advantageous filing status?
choices: Qualifying surviving spouse
Single
Head of household
Married filing separately
questions.exp: A married taxpayer is considered unmarried if the spouse was not in the home during the last six months of the year and the taxpayer maintains a home for a dependent child, so Mona may file as head of household. Single status is never available to someone legally married at year-end.

questions.q: Ned and Olga's daughter, age 22, was a full-time college student for nine months of the year and lived at home except while at school. She earned $15,000 from part-time jobs but did not provide more than half of her own support. Can her parents claim her as a dependent?
choices: Yes, as a qualifying child; her gross income does not matter
No, because her gross income exceeds the qualifying relative limit
No, because she is over age 19
Yes, but only as a qualifying relative
questions.exp: A full-time student under 24 meets the qualifying child age test, and there is no gross income test for a qualifying child. The gross income limit applies only to qualifying relatives, which is the tempting trap.

questions.q: Pam provides more than half the support of her widowed father, who lives in his own apartment. During the year he received $6,000 of taxable interest and $10,000 of Social Security benefits, none of which is taxable. Assume the qualifying relative gross income limit is $5,200. Can Pam claim her father as a dependent?
choices: No, because his $6,000 of taxable interest exceeds the gross income limit
Yes, because only taxable Social Security counts and his is $0
Yes, because a parent is exempt from the gross income test
