No, because his $16,000 of total receipts exceeds the gross income limit
questions.exp: The gross income test counts only items includible in gross income, so nontaxable Social Security is ignored, but the $6,000 of taxable interest alone exceeds the $5,200 limit. Counting all $16,000 reaches the right conclusion for the wrong reason.

questions.q: Rose, age 80, is supported by her three children and herself: Ann provides 35%, Bob 30%, Cal 25%, and Rose 10% from her own savings. Rose has no gross income and meets the other dependency tests. Who may claim Rose as a dependent?
choices: Any one of the three children, if the other two sign statements agreeing not to claim her
Only Ann, because she provided the most support
No one, because no individual provided more than half of her support
Ann or Bob only, because each provided at least 30% of her support
questions.exp: Under a multiple support agreement, any member of a group that together provides more than half the support may claim the dependent if that person provides over 10% and the other over-10% contributors consent. All three children exceed 10%, so any one may be designated.

questions.q: Sam, age 12, is his parents' dependent and has $5,000 of interest and dividend income and no earned income. Assume the dependent standard deduction is $1,350 and the kiddie tax applies to net unearned income above $2,700. How much of Sam's income is taxed at his parents' marginal rate?
questions.exp: Net unearned income is unearned income less twice the $1,350 amount: $5,000 - $2,700 = $2,300, which is taxed at the parents' rate. Subtracting only the standard deduction gives $3,650.

questions.q: Tia, a single taxpayer, is 67 years old and legally blind. Assume the basic standard deduction for a single filer is $15,000 and the additional standard deduction for age or blindness is $2,000 for each condition. Ignore any other deductions for seniors. What is Tia's standard deduction?
questions.exp: A single taxpayer adds the additional amount once for being 65 or older and once for blindness: $15,000 + 2 x $2,000 = $19,000. Allowing only one additional amount gives $17,000.

questions.q: Uri, a single taxpayer, has taxable income of $60,000, all ordinary income. Assume the rates are 10% on taxable income up to $11,925, 12% from $11,925 to $48,475, and 22% from $48,475 to $103,350. What is Uri's regular income tax?

Vic, a single taxpayer, has taxable income of $60,000, which includes $20,000 of qualified dividends; the rest is ordinary income. Assume the 0% rate on qualified dividends applies to taxable income up to $48,350 and the 15% rate applies above that. What is the tax on Vic's qualified dividends?
questions.exp: Ordinary income of $40,000 fills the bottom brackets first; dividends from $40,000 to $48,350 ($8,350) are taxed at 0% and the remaining $11,650 at 15%, or $1,747.50. Taxing all $20,000 at 15% gives $3,000.

questions.q: Wes's prior-year return showed AGI of $200,000 and total tax of $30,000. He expects current-year tax of $50,000. What is the minimum total amount of withholding and timely estimated payments Wes must make to avoid an underpayment penalty?
questions.exp: Required payments are the lesser of 90% of current-year tax ($45,000) or 100% of prior-year tax, increased to 110% when prior-year AGI exceeds $150,000 (110% x $30,000 = $33,000). Using 100% of the prior year gives $30,000.

questions.q: Yara, a single taxpayer, has modified AGI of $230,000, which includes $50,000 of net investment income. The net investment income tax threshold for single filers is $200,000. What is Yara's net investment income tax?
questions.exp: The 3.8% tax applies to the lesser of net investment income ($50,000) or modified AGI over the threshold ($30,000): 3.8% x $30,000 = $1,140. Applying 3.8% to all $50,000 gives $1,900.

questions.q: Zane and Zelda file jointly. Zane earned wages of $180,000 and Zelda earned wages of $120,000 from separate employers, and neither employer withheld additional Medicare tax. The additional Medicare tax threshold is $250,000 for joint filers and the employer withholding threshold is $200,000 per employee. What is their additional Medicare tax liability?
questions.exp: The 0.9% tax applies to combined wages over the $250,000 joint threshold: 0.9% x $50,000 = $450, payable on the return even though no employer withheld it. Using the $200,000 withholding threshold gives $900.

questions.q: Rita and Sam are married and file separate returns. Rita itemizes deductions of $8,000. Sam's itemized deductions total $2,000. Assume the standard deduction for married filing separately is $15,000. What deduction from AGI may Sam claim?
questions.exp: When one spouse filing separately itemizes, the other spouse's standard deduction is zero, so Sam must itemize and deducts his $2,000. Claiming the $15,000 standard deduction is not allowed.

questions.q: Tina, age 7, lives all year with her mother (AGI $30,000) and her grandmother (AGI $50,000). Tina is a qualifying child of both, and both claim her as a dependent on their returns. Under the tie-breaker rules, who is entitled to claim Tina?
choices: Whoever files first
The mother, because a parent has priority over a nonparent
Neither, because Tina is a qualifying child of two taxpayers
The grandmother, because her AGI is higher
questions.exp: When a parent and a nonparent both claim the same qualifying child, the parent wins. The higher-AGI rule applies only when no parent claims the child (or between two parents, by residence then AGI).

questions.q: Una is divorced and has custody of her son all year. She signs a written release allowing her former husband to claim the son as a dependent. Which of the following tax benefits may the former husband claim for the son?
choices: The child and dependent care credit
The child tax credit
The earned income credit
Head of household filing status
questions.exp: A release of the dependency claim lets the noncustodial parent claim the child as a dependent and take the child tax credit. Head of household status, the earned income credit and the dependent care credit stay with the custodial parent because they depend on where the child lives.

questions.q: Vera, age 20, a full-time student, married during the year. She and her husband filed a joint return solely to obtain a $400 refund of income tax withheld; neither would have had a tax liability on separate returns. Her parents meet all other tests to claim her. May her parents claim Vera as a dependent?
choices: No, because a full-time student over 19 cannot be a qualifying child
Yes, because the joint return was filed only to claim a refund and no tax liability would exist on separate returns
No, because a married individual who files a joint return can never be claimed as a dependent
Yes, but only if the parents also provide over half of her husband's support
questions.exp: The joint return test is not violated when the joint return is filed only to claim a refund and no tax liability would exist for either spouse on separate returns. Students under 24 can still be qualifying children.

questions.q: Will, a single taxpayer, had wages of $70,000, taxable interest of $2,000 and a $5,000 long-term capital loss with no capital gains. He made a $4,000 deductible traditional IRA contribution. What is Will's adjusted gross income?
questions.exp: AGI is $70,000 + $2,000 - $3,000 (net capital loss deduction limit) - $4,000 IRA deduction = $65,000, with $2,000 of capital loss carried forward. Deducting the full $5,000 loss gives $63,000.

questions.q: Xia is unmarried and provides all the support for her cousin, who lived with Xia as a member of her household for the entire year and has no gross income. What is Xia's filing status?
choices: Head of household, because the cousin has no gross income
Head of household, because she supports a dependent who lives with her
Single, because a cousin can never be claimed as a dependent
Single, because a cousin who qualifies as a dependent only by living in her household is not a qualifying person for head of household
questions.exp: Xia can claim the cousin as a qualifying relative under the member-of-household test, but a dependent who qualifies only through that test is not a qualifying person for head of household. Assuming every dependent supports head of household status is the trap.

questions.q: Yale, age 20, is a full-time student. His support for the year was $25,000: $12,000 of tuition paid by a scholarship, $8,000 paid by his parents and $5,000 from his summer job earnings. He lives with his parents when not at school. Is Yale his parents' qualifying child?
choices: Yes, because a scholarship received by a full-time student is not counted in determining whether he provided over half of his own support
No, because his own earnings plus his scholarship exceed half of his support
No, because his parents did not provide over half of his total support
Yes, because there is no support test for a qualifying child
questions.exp: Scholarships of a full-time student are disregarded for the self-support test, so Yale provided only $5,000 of $13,000; he did not provide over half his own support. A qualifying child does have a support test (the child must not self-support), and the parents need not provide over half.

questions.q: Zoe, a single taxpayer in the 37% bracket, sold gold coins she had held for three years at a $10,000 gain. She has no other capital transactions. What is the maximum federal income tax on the gain, ignoring the net investment income tax?
questions.exp: Long-term gain on collectibles is taxed at a maximum 28% rate: 28% x $10,000 = $2,800. Applying the 20% maximum rate for other long-term capital gains gives $2,000.

questions.q: Amy's husband died in March of the current year. She has not remarried and has no children or other dependents. What are Amy's filing statuses for the current year and the following year?
choices: Head of household for both years
Married filing jointly for the current year; single for the following year
Married filing jointly for the current year; qualifying surviving spouse for the following year
Single for both years
questions.exp: A surviving spouse may file jointly for the year of death; afterward, qualifying surviving spouse status requires a dependent child, so Amy files as single the next year. Choosing qualifying surviving spouse overlooks the dependent child requirement.

questions.q: Ben, age 16, is his parents' dependent. He earned $8,000 of wages and $1,000 of interest. Assume the dependent standard deduction is the greater of $1,350 or earned income plus $450, not to exceed the regular standard deduction of $15,000. What is Ben's taxable income?
questions.exp: His standard deduction is $8,000 + $450 = $8,450, so taxable income is $9,000 - $8,450 = $550. Using the full $15,000 standard deduction available to non-dependents gives $0.

questions.q: Cara is a U.S. citizen. She provides all the support for her mother, a citizen and resident of Mexico who has never lived in the United States and has no gross income. May Cara claim her mother as a dependent?
choices: Yes, because a resident of Mexico meets the citizenship or residency test
Yes, but only if her mother becomes a U.S. resident before year-end
No, because a dependent must be a U.S. citizen or resident
No, because a parent must live with the taxpayer to be a qualifying relative
questions.exp: The citizenship or residency test is met by U.S. citizens, nationals and residents, and by residents of Canada or Mexico. A parent need not live with the taxpayer to be a qualifying relative.

questions.q: Dale has net earnings from self-employment of $50,000 from his sole proprietorship and no wages. Assume self-employment tax is 15.3% of 92.35% of net earnings. What is Dale's self-employment tax?
questions.exp: SE tax is $50,000 x 92.35% x 15.3% = $7,065 (rounded). Applying 15.3% to the full $50,000 ignores the 92.35% adjustment and gives $7,650; $3,532 is only the deductible half.

questions.q: Eve's son, age 30, is permanently and totally disabled and lives with her all year. He earns $7,000 at a sheltered workshop and does not provide over half of his own support. Assume the qualifying relative gross income limit is $5,200. May Eve claim her son as a dependent?
choices: Yes, as a qualifying child, because the age test does not apply to a permanently and totally disabled child
No, because his gross income exceeds the qualifying relative limit
Yes, but only as a qualifying relative
No, because he is over the age limit for a qualifying child
questions.exp: A permanently and totally disabled child meets the qualifying child age test at any age, and qualifying children have no gross income test. Testing him as a qualifying relative would fail the $5,200 gross income limit.

questions.q: Fay, unmarried, lives with her dependent 9-year-old daughter. The household's costs for the year were rent $12,000, utilities $3,000, groceries consumed in the home $6,000, clothing $2,000 and medical care $1,000. Fay paid $12,000 of these costs and her parents paid the rest. What is the cost of maintaining the household, and does Fay qualify for head of household status?
choices: $24,000; she does not qualify because she paid only half
$21,000; she qualifies because she paid more than half
$15,000; she qualifies because she paid more than half
$23,000; she qualifies because she paid more than half
questions.exp: Household costs include rent, utilities and food eaten in the home ($21,000) but not clothing or medical care, so Fay's $12,000 is more than half. Including all $24,000 makes her share exactly half, which would fail the more-than-half test.

questions.q: Gil and Hope filed a joint return. After the IRS assessed additional tax attributable to Gil's unreported business income, Hope asked who is liable. Absent innocent spouse relief, what is the rule for joint filers?
choices: Liability is split equally between the spouses
Each spouse is jointly and severally liable for the entire tax, interest and penalties
Each spouse is liable only for tax on his or her own income
The spouse who earned more income is solely liable
questions.exp: Spouses who file jointly are jointly and severally liable for the full tax, interest and penalties on the return, so the IRS may collect the entire amount from either. Limiting liability to one's own income requires relief such as innocent spouse or separation of liability.

questions.q: Ivy and Jake married on December 31 of the current year. Neither has any dependents. Which filing statuses are available to them for the current year?
choices: Head of household
Married filing jointly or married filing separately
Single
Single for one spouse and married filing separately for the other
questions.exp: Marital status is determined on the last day of the year, so a couple married on December 31 is treated as married for the whole year and must file jointly or separately. Single status is unavailable to either spouse.

questions.q: Mark and Nora file jointly and have two qualifying children, ages 6 and 9. Their modified AGI is $412,500. Assume the child tax credit is $2,200 per qualifying child and is reduced by $50 for each $1,000 (or fraction thereof) of modified AGI above $400,000. What is their child tax credit?
questions.exp: The excess of $12,500 is rounded up to 13 increments of $1,000, so the reduction is 13 x $50 = $650 and the credit is $4,400 - $650 = $3,750. Using 12.5 increments without rounding up gives $3,775.

questions.q: Opal and Paul file jointly. Their dependents are their son, age 16; their daughter, who turned 17 in November; and Paul's widowed mother, who lives with them. Assume the child tax credit is $2,200 per qualifying child, the credit for other dependents is $500 per dependent, and their AGI is well below the phase-out threshold. What is their total child tax credit and credit for other dependents?
questions.exp: Only a child under 17 at year-end is a qualifying child for the child tax credit ($2,200); the 17-year-old and the mother each generate the $500 credit for other dependents: $2,200 + $500 + $500 = $3,200. Counting the 17-year-old as a qualifying child gives $4,900.

questions.q: Rick and Sue file jointly and paid $7,000 of qualifying child care for their two children, ages 3 and 5, so they could work. Rick earned $40,000 and Sue earned $5,000 from part-time work. Assume the expense limit is $6,000 for two or more qualifying persons and the applicable credit percentage is 20%. What is their child and dependent care credit?
questions.exp: Qualifying expenses are limited to the lesser of actual costs, the $6,000 cap, or the lower-earning spouse's earned income ($5,000), so the credit is 20% x $5,000 = $1,000. Ignoring the earned income limit gives $1,200.

questions.q: Ted and Uma, who file jointly, paid $8,000 of graduate tuition for each of their two children during the year. Their AGI is below the phase-out range. Assume the lifetime learning credit is 20% of up to $10,000 of qualified expenses. What is their maximum lifetime learning credit?
questions.exp: The lifetime learning credit is computed per taxpayer return, not per student: 20% x the $10,000 cap = $2,000. Applying the cap to each student separately gives $3,200.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the American opportunity tax credit is correct?
choices: Its maximum is a single amount per taxpayer regardless of the number of eligible students
It may be claimed for any number of years of postsecondary education
Up to 40% of the credit may be refundable
It applies to graduate school tuition after the first four years of postsecondary education
questions.exp: Up to 40% of the American opportunity credit is refundable. The credit is computed per eligible student and is limited to the first four years of postsecondary education; the per-return cap and unlimited years describe the lifetime learning credit.

questions.q: Vera's U.S. tax liability before credits is $30,000 on worldwide taxable income of $150,000, of which $50,000 is foreign-source taxable income. She paid $12,000 of foreign income taxes. What is Vera's foreign tax credit for the year?
questions.exp: The credit is limited to U.S. tax x foreign-source taxable income / worldwide taxable income: $30,000 x $50,000 / $150,000 = $10,000; the $2,000 excess carries back one year and forward ten. Crediting all $12,000 ignores the §904 limitation.

questions.q: Wendy has a qualifying child and earned income that would otherwise entitle her to the earned income credit. She also has $12,500 of interest and dividend income. Assume the disqualified investment income limit for the year is $11,950. What earned income credit may Wendy claim?
choices: $0, because her investment income exceeds the limit
The credit reduced by the $550 of investment income over the limit
The full credit computed from her earned income
50% of the credit computed from her earned income
questions.exp: If disqualified investment income exceeds the annual limit by any amount, no earned income credit is allowed; it is a cliff, not a phase-out. Reducing the credit by the excess treats the rule as a phase-out.

questions.q: Xena, whose AGI qualifies her for a 20% retirement savings contributions (saver's) credit rate, contributed $2,500 to her traditional IRA. Assume the credit applies to a maximum of $2,000 of contributions per person, and she received no retirement distributions. What is her saver's credit?
questions.exp: The credit is the applicable rate times contributions up to the $2,000 cap: 20% x $2,000 = $400. Applying 20% to the full $2,500 contribution gives $500.

questions.q: Which of the following individual credits is refundable?
choices: The lifetime learning credit
The child and dependent care credit
The foreign tax credit
The earned income credit
questions.exp: The earned income credit is refundable, so it can produce a refund in excess of tax liability. The dependent care, lifetime learning and foreign tax credits are nonrefundable (the foreign tax credit has carryovers instead).

questions.q: During the year Yolanda earned wages of $120,000 from one employer and $90,000 from a second, unrelated employer, and each employer withheld 6.2% Social Security tax on all wages paid. Assume the Social Security wage base is $176,100. What credit for excess Social Security tax withheld can Yolanda claim on her return?
questions.exp: Total withheld is $7,440 + $5,580 = $13,020, but the maximum employee tax is 6.2% x $176,100 = $10,918.20, so $2,101.80 is credited on her return. Each employer withheld correctly, but the excess arises from combining two employers' wages.

questions.q: Zeke, a single taxpayer, has alternative minimum taxable income of $600,000. Assume the AMT exemption is $90,000, reduced by 50% of AMTI in excess of $500,000. What is Zeke's AMT exemption?
questions.exp: The exemption is reduced by 50% x ($600,000 - $500,000) = $50,000, leaving $40,000. Using a 25% phase-out rate gives $65,000.

questions.q: Abe itemizes. His taxable income is $200,000 after deducting state and local taxes of $10,000, qualified home acquisition mortgage interest of $15,000 and charitable contributions of $8,000. He also received $5,000 of tax-exempt interest on specified private activity bonds. He has no other adjustments or preferences. What is Abe's alternative minimum taxable income before the exemption?
questions.exp: For AMT, state and local taxes are added back ($10,000) and private activity bond interest is a preference ($5,000): $200,000 + $15,000 = $215,000. Qualified acquisition mortgage interest and charitable contributions remain deductible, so adding them back gives $238,000.

questions.q: Beth, a single taxpayer, claimed a $15,000 standard deduction and reported taxable income of $100,000. She has no other AMT adjustments or preferences. What is her alternative minimum taxable income before the exemption?
questions.exp: The standard deduction is not allowed in computing AMTI, so it is added back: $100,000 + $15,000 = $115,000. Assuming a taxpayer who does not itemize has no AMT adjustments gives $100,000.

questions.q: Carl exercised incentive stock options to buy 1,000 shares of his employer's stock at $10 per share when the stock was worth $35 per share. He held the shares at year-end. What is Carl's AMT adjustment for the year from this exercise?
questions.exp: No regular tax income arises on exercise of an ISO, but the bargain element is a positive AMT adjustment: ($35 - $10) x 1,000 = $25,000. The $0 answer is the regular tax result only.

questions.q: Two years after exercising incentive stock options for 1,000 shares at $10 per share when the stock was worth $35 per share (and reporting the related AMT adjustment), Carl sold the shares for $50 per share in a qualifying disposition. What gain does Carl report for regular tax and for AMT purposes in the year of sale?
choices: $15,000 regular tax gain; $40,000 AMT gain
$40,000 gain for both regular tax and AMT
$15,000 gain for both regular tax and AMT
$40,000 regular tax gain; $15,000 AMT gain
questions.exp: Regular tax basis is the $10 exercise price, giving a $40,000 gain, while AMT basis includes the $25,000 adjustment ($35 per share), giving a $15,000 AMT gain (a $25,000 negative adjustment). Using the same basis for both double-counts the earlier AMT adjustment.

questions.q: Which of the following AMT items can give rise to a minimum tax credit usable against regular tax in later years?
choices: The add-back of state and local taxes
The bargain element on exercise of an incentive stock option
Tax-exempt interest on specified private activity bonds
The add-back of the standard deduction
questions.exp: The minimum tax credit arises only from deferral items, such as the ISO adjustment, which reverses when the stock is sold. Exclusion items such as the taxes add-back, private activity bond interest and standard deduction never reverse and create no credit.

questions.q: Which of the following creates an AMT depreciation adjustment for property placed in service this year?
choices: Bonus depreciation on qualifying equipment
Straight-line MACRS on a commercial building
Straight-line MACRS on residential rental property
200% declining-balance MACRS on 7-year equipment, with no bonus depreciation claimed
questions.exp: For AMT, personal property depreciated at 200% declining balance must use 150% declining balance, creating an adjustment. Straight-line real property depreciation and bonus depreciation are allowed the same for AMT, so they create no adjustment.

questions.q: Dee, a single taxpayer, has AMTI of $300,000 and regular tax of $50,000. Assume her AMT exemption is $90,000 with no phase-out at her income level, the AMT rate is 26% on the first $239,100 of the AMT base and 28% above that, and she has no capital gains or AMT foreign tax credit. What is Dee's alternative minimum tax?
questions.exp: The AMT base is $300,000 - $90,000 = $210,000, all taxed at 26%, so tentative minimum tax is $54,600 and AMT is the $4,600 excess over regular tax. The $54,600 figure is tentative minimum tax, not the additional AMT owed.

questions.q: Earl has one qualifying child, earned income of $12,500 and a regular tax liability of $0. Assume the refundable additional child tax credit equals 15% of earned income over $2,500, limited to $1,700 per qualifying child. What refundable child tax credit may Earl claim?
questions.exp: The refundable portion is the lesser of $1,700 or 15% x ($12,500 - $2,500) = $1,500. Claiming the $1,700 maximum ignores the earned income formula.

questions.q: Fran and her husband both work full time and have a 10-year-old son. Which of the following payments is a qualifying expense for the child and dependent care credit?
choices: Overnight summer camp for the son
Day camp for the son while both parents work
Private school tuition for the son's fifth-grade year
Payments to their 17-year-old daughter to babysit the son
questions.exp: Day camp for a child under 13 that enables the parents to work qualifies. Overnight camp and kindergarten-or-higher tuition do not, and payments to the taxpayer's own child under age 19 are excluded.

questions.q: Gus, a first-year college student whose parents claim him as a dependent, paid $1,500 of tuition to the college and $600 for required textbooks he bought online, plus $5,000 for a dormitory room. His parents' AGI is below the phase-out range. Assume the American opportunity credit equals 100% of the first $2,000 of qualified expenses plus 25% of the next $2,000. What American opportunity credit may his parents claim?
questions.exp: Qualified expenses include tuition and required course materials even if not bought from the school ($2,100), but not room and board: $2,000 + 25% x $100 = $2,025. Excluding the textbooks gives $1,500.

questions.q: Hana, a single taxpayer, would qualify for a $2,500 American opportunity credit before any phase-out. Her modified AGI is $84,000. Assume the credit phases out ratably for single filers with modified AGI between $80,000 and $90,000. What is her allowable credit?
questions.exp: Modified AGI is 40% through the $10,000 phase-out range, so the credit is $2,500 x 60% = $1,500. The $1,000 figure is the disallowed amount.

questions.q: Ian earned $60,000 in wages. His wife was a full-time student for nine months of the year and had no earnings. They paid $4,000 of qualifying care for their one child and file jointly. Assume the expense limit for one qualifying person is $3,000, a full-time student spouse is deemed to earn $250 per month with one qualifying person, and the credit rate is 20%. What is their child and dependent care credit?
questions.exp: The student spouse's deemed earned income is $250 x 9 = $2,250, which caps qualifying expenses: 20% x $2,250 = $450. Using the $3,000 expense limit ignores the earned income limitation.

questions.q: Jill paid $1,000 of foreign income tax on foreign investment income. Her marginal U.S. tax rate is 24%, and the foreign tax credit limitation is not a factor. By how much more does claiming the foreign tax credit reduce her U.S. tax than deducting the foreign tax as an itemized deduction?
questions.exp: A credit reduces tax dollar for dollar ($1,000), while a deduction saves only 24% x $1,000 = $240, a difference of $760. The $240 figure is the value of the deduction, not the difference.

questions.q: Kim and Lou, who both work, paid $8,000 of qualifying day care for their two young children. Kim excluded $5,000 under her employer's dependent care assistance program. Assume the expense limit for two qualifying persons is $6,000 and the credit rate is 20%. What is their child and dependent care credit?
questions.exp: The $6,000 limit is reduced by the $5,000 excluded under the employer plan, leaving $1,000 x 20% = $200. Applying 20% to the $3,000 of expenses not reimbursed gives $600, which ignores the reduction of the cap.

questions.q: Which statement about net capital gain under the individual alternative minimum tax is correct?
choices: Qualified dividends and net capital gain keep the same preferential rates under the AMT as under the regular tax
Net capital gain is added back as a tax preference item
Net capital gain is excluded from AMTI
Net capital gain is taxed at the 26% and 28% AMT rates
questions.exp: The AMT computation taxes net capital gain and qualified dividends at the same 0/15/20% rates used for regular tax, with only the remaining AMT base taxed at 26%/28%. Net capital gain is included in AMTI, not excluded or treated as a preference.

questions.q: Mia and Ned file jointly with AGI below all phase-out ranges. Their daughter, a first-year undergraduate, had $4,000 of qualified tuition, and Ned took a graduate course costing $5,000. Assume the American opportunity credit is 100% of the first $2,000 plus 25% of the next $2,000 per student, and the lifetime learning credit is 20% of up to $10,000 of expenses. What is their maximum total education credit?
questions.exp: Different credits may be claimed for different students in the same year: an American opportunity credit of $2,500 for the daughter plus a lifetime learning credit of 20% x $5,000 = $1,000 for Ned, for $3,500. Using only the lifetime learning credit on all $9,000 gives $1,800.

questions.q: Opal's regular tax liability before credits is $1,200, and she qualifies for a $2,000 lifetime learning credit. She has no other credits. What is the result?
choices: Her tax is reduced to $0 and the $800 excess is lost
Her tax is reduced to $0 and the $800 excess is carried forward
Her tax is reduced to $0 and the $800 excess is carried back one year
Her tax is reduced to $0 and the $800 excess is refunded
questions.exp: The lifetime learning credit is nonrefundable and has no carryover, so it can reduce tax only to zero and the excess is lost. Refund treatment applies only to refundable credits such as the earned income credit.

questions.q: Pete exercised nonqualified stock options and acquired employer stock with a $25,000 spread between fair market value and exercise price. The stock had a readily ascertainable value. How is the exercise treated?
choices: $25,000 of ordinary income for regular tax and no AMT adjustment
No income for regular tax or AMT until the shares are sold
$25,000 of ordinary income for regular tax and a $25,000 positive AMT adjustment
No regular tax income and a $25,000 positive AMT adjustment
questions.exp: The spread on a nonqualified option is compensation income on exercise under §83 for both regular tax and AMT, so no AMT adjustment is needed. The positive AMT adjustment with no regular income describes an incentive stock option.

questions.q: Quinn, a U.S. citizen working abroad, earned $150,000 of foreign wages, of which he excluded $130,000 under the foreign earned income exclusion. He paid $30,000 of foreign income tax on the wages. Assume the overall foreign tax credit limitation is not binding. What foreign tax credit may Quinn claim?
questions.exp: No credit is allowed for foreign taxes allocable to excluded income, so only $30,000 x $20,000 / $150,000 = $4,000 is creditable. Claiming the full $30,000 would give a double benefit on the excluded wages.

questions.q: Ellen, who itemizes, has AGI of $80,000. During the year she paid the following unreimbursed amounts: physician fees $5,000, prescription drugs $1,200, over-the-counter vitamins $300, health insurance premiums paid with after-tax dollars $2,800, and elective cosmetic surgery $3,000. Assume the medical expense floor is 7.5% of AGI. What is Ellen's medical expense deduction?
questions.exp: Qualifying expenses are $5,000 + $1,200 + $2,800 = $9,000 (nonprescription vitamins and elective cosmetic surgery do not qualify), less 7.5% x $80,000 = $6,000, leaving $3,000. Including the vitamins gives $3,300.

questions.q: Frank, who itemizes, paid the following during the year: state income tax $22,000, real estate tax on his home $15,000, real estate tax on vacation land in Mexico $3,000, state sales tax $4,000, and a $500 vehicle registration fee based entirely on the car's value. Assume the deduction limit for state and local taxes is $40,000 and Frank's income is below any phase-down threshold. What is Frank's maximum itemized deduction for taxes?
questions.exp: Frank deducts the greater of income or sales tax ($22,000), home real estate tax ($15,000) and the value-based registration fee ($500) = $37,500; foreign real property taxes are not deductible. Including the Mexican property tax pushes the total to $40,500 and the cap of $40,000 looks like the answer.

questions.q: Gail borrowed $900,000 in 2020 to buy her principal residence, secured by the home, and the balance stayed at $900,000 throughout the year. She paid $45,000 of interest on the loan. Assume the acquisition indebtedness limit is $750,000. How much of the interest is deductible as qualified residence interest?
questions.exp: Interest is deductible only on the portion of acquisition debt within the limit: $45,000 x $750,000 / $900,000 = $37,500. Deducting all $45,000 ignores the debt limit.

questions.q: Hank, whose AGI is $100,000, donated to a public charity common stock he had held for three years. The stock had a fair market value of $40,000 and a basis of $10,000. Hank made no special election and made no other contributions. Disregard any percentage-of-AGI reduction to charitable deductions. What is Hank's charitable contribution deduction for the year?
choices: $10,000 this year, with no carryover
$30,000 this year, with no carryover
$40,000 this year
$30,000 this year, with a $10,000 carryover
questions.exp: Long-term capital gain property given to a public charity is deductible at fair market value but limited to 30% of AGI ($30,000), with the $10,000 excess carried forward up to five years. Deducting $40,000 ignores the 30% ceiling.

questions.q: Iris donated to her church stock she had purchased eight months earlier for $3,000. On the date of the gift the stock was worth $5,000. Her AGI is large enough that no percentage limitation applies, and any AGI-based floor should be disregarded. What is Iris's charitable contribution deduction?
questions.exp: Property that would produce short-term gain if sold is ordinary income property, so the deduction is limited to basis ($3,000). Deducting fair market value applies only to long-term capital gain property.

questions.q: Jack's personal residence, located in a federally declared disaster area, was damaged by a hurricane. The home's adjusted basis was $50,000; its value was $80,000 before and $20,000 after the storm. Insurance paid $10,000. Jack's AGI is $100,000. Assume the $100 per-casualty floor and the 10%-of-AGI floor apply. What is Jack's casualty loss deduction?
questions.exp: The loss is the lesser of the $60,000 decline in value or $50,000 basis, less $10,000 insurance = $40,000, less $100 = $39,900, less $10,000 (10% of AGI) = $29,900. The $39,900 figure omits the 10%-of-AGI floor.

questions.q: Kara, a self-employed consultant, has net earnings from her sole proprietorship of $100,000 and computes self-employment tax of $14,130. She has no wages. What deduction for AGI does Kara get with respect to her self-employment tax?
questions.exp: §164 allows a deduction for AGI equal to one-half of self-employment tax: $14,130 / 2 = $7,065, reflecting the employer-equivalent portion. Deducting the full tax overstates the adjustment.

questions.q: Leah is covered only by a self-only high-deductible health plan through her employer. Her employer contributed $1,000 to her health savings account, and Leah contributed $4,000 on her own. Assume the annual HSA contribution limit for self-only coverage is $4,300. What deduction for AGI may Leah claim for her HSA contribution?
questions.exp: Employer contributions count toward the annual limit, so Leah may deduct only $4,300 - $1,000 = $3,300; the $700 excess is subject to excise tax unless withdrawn. Deducting her full $4,000 ignores the employer's contribution.

questions.q: Mike, a single taxpayer, paid $3,000 of interest on qualified student loans this year. His modified AGI is $90,000. Assume the maximum deduction is $2,500 and the phase-out range for single filers is $85,000 to $100,000. What is Mike's student loan interest deduction?
questions.exp: The $2,500 maximum is reduced by ($90,000 - $85,000) / $15,000 = one-third, or $833, leaving $1,667. The $833 figure is the reduction, not the allowed deduction.

questions.q: Nina, a single taxpayer age 40, is an active participant in her employer's 401(k) plan. She contributed $7,000 to a traditional IRA. Her modified AGI is $83,000. Assume the IRA contribution limit is $7,000 and the deduction phase-out range for active participants is $79,000 to $89,000. What is Nina's deductible IRA contribution?
questions.exp: The deduction is reduced by ($83,000 - $79,000) / $10,000 = 40% of $7,000 = $2,800, leaving $4,200 deductible. The $2,800 figure is the disallowed portion.

questions.q: Omar, a self-employed architect with net profit of $50,000, paid $800 per month for his own health insurance for the entire year. From October through December he was eligible to participate in a subsidized health plan through his spouse's employer but did not enroll. What is Omar's self-employed health insurance deduction?
questions.exp: The deduction for AGI is not allowed for any month the taxpayer is eligible for an employer-subsidized plan, including a spouse's, so only 9 months x $800 = $7,200 qualifies. Actual enrollment is not required to lose those months.

questions.q: Pia, a single taxpayer, has qualified business income of $80,000 from a sole proprietorship that is not a specified service business. Her taxable income before the qualified business income deduction is $70,000, which includes $10,000 of net capital gain. Assume her taxable income is below the threshold at which the wage and property limitations apply. What is Pia's qualified business income deduction?
questions.exp: The §199A deduction is the lesser of 20% of QBI ($16,000) or 20% of taxable income reduced by net capital gain (20% x $60,000 = $12,000). Forgetting to remove net capital gain gives $14,000.

questions.q: Which of the following is deductible in arriving at adjusted gross income?
choices: Unreimbursed business expenses of an employee who is not a reservist, performing artist or fee-basis official
Contributions made directly by the taxpayer to a health savings account
Home mortgage interest
Unreimbursed medical expenses
questions.exp: Direct HSA contributions are an above-the-line adjustment under §62. Mortgage interest and medical expenses are itemized deductions, and most employees' unreimbursed business expenses are not deductible at all.

questions.q: Quin paid $12,000 of interest on a margin loan used to buy stocks and bonds. His investment income consisted of $5,000 of taxable interest and $3,000 of qualified dividends; he did not elect to treat any qualified dividends as ordinary income. He has no investment expenses. What is Quin's investment interest expense deduction for the year?
questions.exp: Investment interest is deductible only to the extent of net investment income, which excludes qualified dividends taxed at capital gain rates unless an election is made, so the limit is $5,000 and $7,000 carries forward. Including the dividends gives $8,000.

questions.q: Rob volunteered 100 hours at a qualified charity; his normal billing rate is $50 per hour. He also spent $300 on supplies used in his volunteer work and paid $200 for a ticket to the charity's fundraising dinner, which had a fair market value of $80. Disregard any AGI-based floor or ceiling. What is Rob's charitable contribution deduction?
questions.exp: The value of donated services is never deductible, but unreimbursed out-of-pocket costs ($300) and the excess of the dinner payment over its value ($200 - $80 = $120) are, for $420. Deducting the full $200 ticket ignores the quid pro quo benefit.

questions.q: On her physician's advice, Sue installed an elevator in her home because of a heart condition, at a cost of $20,000. An appraiser determined the elevator increased the home's value by $12,000. How much of the cost qualifies as a medical expense before applying the AGI floor?
questions.exp: A medically necessary capital improvement qualifies only to the extent its cost exceeds the increase in the property's value: $20,000 - $12,000 = $8,000. The $12,000 increase in value is added to the home's basis instead.

questions.q: On July 1, Tia refinanced the mortgage on her principal residence with a new 30-year loan and paid $3,600 of points. None of the proceeds were used to improve the home. How much of the points may Tia deduct this year?
questions.exp: Points on a refinancing must be amortized over the loan term: $3,600 / 360 months = $10 per month x 6 months = $60. Only points paid to buy or improve a principal residence are deductible in full when paid.

questions.q: Uma actively participates in managing a rental house that produced a $30,000 loss this year. She has no other passive income, and her modified AGI is $120,000. Under the rental real estate exception, the $25,000 allowance is reduced by 50% of modified AGI over $100,000. How much of the rental loss may Uma deduct this year?
questions.exp: The §469 allowance is $25,000 - 50% x ($120,000 - $100,000) = $15,000, and the remaining $15,000 is suspended. The $10,000 figure is the reduction, not the allowance.

questions.q: Vic, a self-employed consultant, spent $400 on a business dinner with a client at which business was discussed and $600 on a round of golf with the same client. Neither was lavish. How much may Vic deduct?
questions.exp: Business meals are 50% deductible ($200), while entertainment such as golf is not deductible at all under §274. Applying the 50% rule to both gives $500.

questions.q: Wanda, a self-employed sales representative, gave holiday gifts to 10 clients. Each gift cost $40, plus $3 per gift for engraving. What is Wanda's deduction for business gifts?
questions.exp: Business gifts are limited to $25 per recipient per year, but incidental costs such as engraving are not counted toward the limit: 10 x ($25 + $3) = $280. Applying the cap to the engraving too gives $250.

questions.q: Yuri, a self-employed graphic designer with a large net profit, uses a 350-square-foot room in his home regularly and exclusively as his principal place of business. He elects the simplified home office method, which allows $5 per square foot for up to 300 square feet. What is his home office deduction?
questions.exp: Under the simplified method the deduction is $5 x the lesser of actual square footage or 300 square feet = $1,500. Using all 350 square feet gives $1,750.

questions.q: Zack and Zoe file jointly. Their itemized deductions are state and local taxes $12,000 (below the applicable cap), home mortgage interest $14,000 and cash charitable contributions $4,000. Assume their standard deduction is $31,500 and any charitable floor or additional standard-deduction charity amount should be disregarded. What is their deduction from AGI, before any qualified business income deduction?
questions.exp: Taxpayers deduct the greater of itemized deductions ($12,000 + $14,000 + $4,000 = $30,000) or the standard deduction ($31,500). Taking itemized deductions because they are listed ignores the comparison.

questions.q: Abby cashed in a certificate of deposit before maturity. The bank credited $1,000 of interest during the year and charged a $300 early withdrawal penalty. How does Abby report these amounts?
choices: Include $1,000 of interest income and deduct the $300 penalty as an itemized deduction
Include $1,000 of interest income with no deduction for the penalty
Include $1,000 of interest income and deduct the $300 penalty for AGI
Include $700 of interest income, net of the penalty
questions.exp: The full interest is gross income and the forfeited-interest penalty is an above-the-line deduction under §62. Netting the two on the interest line is not permitted.

questions.q: Bart, whose AGI is $200,000, donated a painting he had owned for five years to a local hospital, which placed it in storage and plans to sell it. The painting had a fair market value of $20,000 and a basis of $8,000. Disregard any AGI-based floor. What is Bart's charitable contribution deduction?
questions.exp: For tangible personal property put to a use unrelated to the charity's exempt purpose, the deduction is reduced by the long-term gain, leaving basis ($8,000). The $12,000 figure is the disallowed appreciation.

questions.q: A fire completely destroyed a machine used in Cole's sole proprietorship. The machine had an adjusted basis of $15,000 and a fair market value of $10,000 before the fire. Insurance paid $4,000. What is Cole's deductible casualty loss?
questions.exp: When business property is completely destroyed, the loss is adjusted basis less insurance ($15,000 - $4,000 = $11,000), with no $100 or 10%-of-AGI floor. Using fair market value gives $6,000, and applying the personal floor gives $10,900.

questions.q: Dina, a cash-basis taxpayer not in the business of lending, made a bona fide $5,000 loan to a friend, documented by a promissory note. This year the friend filed bankruptcy and the debt became wholly worthless. How does Dina treat the loss?
choices: A $5,000 ordinary loss deductible for AGI
A $5,000 short-term capital loss
A $5,000 itemized deduction
No deduction, because loans to friends are personal
questions.exp: Under §166, a nonbusiness bad debt is a short-term capital loss when it becomes wholly worthless, deductible against capital gains and then up to $3,000 of ordinary income. Treating it as an ordinary loss applies the business bad debt rule.

questions.q: On April 1 of a non-leap year, Ed bought a house from Fay. The real property tax for the calendar year was $3,650, all of which Ed paid in December. The sale contract did not reapportion the tax. How much real property tax may Ed deduct?
questions.exp: Property tax is apportioned by days: the seller is treated as paying for January 1 through March 31 (90 days x $10 = $900) and the buyer for the remaining 275 days, or $2,750. The $900 Ed paid on Fay's behalf is added to his basis rather than deducted.

questions.q: Gwen's AGI is $50,000. During the year she gave $35,000 in cash to her city's public library foundation, a public charity, and made no other gifts. Assume the 60%-of-AGI limit applies to cash contributions to public charities and disregard any AGI-based floor. What is Gwen's charitable contribution deduction this year?
choices: $25,000, with a $10,000 carryover
$15,000, with a $20,000 carryover
$30,000, with a $5,000 carryover
questions.exp: Cash gifts to public charities are limited to 60% of AGI ($30,000) with a five-year carryover of the $5,000 excess. The other amounts apply the 50% or 30% limits that govern different property or donees.

questions.q: Hal, a sole proprietor with no employees, has net profit of $100,000 and a deduction of $7,065 for one-half of his self-employment tax. He contributes the maximum to a SEP plan, whose limit is 25% of compensation (the dollar cap is not a factor). What is Hal's maximum deductible SEP contribution?
questions.exp: For a self-employed individual, compensation is net earnings less the contribution itself, so the effective rate is 20% of ($100,000 - $7,065) = $18,587. Applying 25% directly to $92,935 gives $23,234.

questions.q: During the year Ida paid $4,000 of health insurance premiums through her employer's pre-tax salary reduction (cafeteria) plan, $2,000 of dental insurance premiums with after-tax dollars, and $1,500 of Medicare Part B premiums. What amount of these premiums counts toward her itemized medical expenses before the AGI floor?
questions.exp: Premiums paid with pre-tax dollars are already excluded from income and cannot also be deducted; the after-tax dental premiums and Medicare Part B premiums qualify: $2,000 + $1,500 = $3,500. Counting the cafeteria plan premiums double-dips.

questions.q: Under a divorce decree executed in 2021, Ann receives $24,000 of alimony and $12,000 of child support from her former spouse during the current year. How much of these payments must Ann include in gross income?
questions.exp: For divorce or separation instruments executed after 2018, alimony is neither deductible by the payer nor includible by the recipient, and child support is never income. Including the $24,000 alimony applies the pre-2019 rule.

questions.q: Lee is the beneficiary of an $80,000 life insurance policy on his late mother. Lee elected to receive the proceeds in ten annual installments of $10,000 each. How much of each $10,000 installment is included in Lee's gross income?
questions.exp: Under §101, the death benefit is prorated over the installments: $80,000 / 10 = $8,000 excluded each year, so the $2,000 interest element is taxable. Treating installments as fully excluded ignores the interest earned on the deferred payout.

questions.q: Pat, an unrelated investor, purchased a $100,000 life insurance policy on the life of Quinn for $20,000 and later paid $5,000 of premiums. On Quinn's death Pat collected the $100,000 face amount. How much must Pat include in gross income?
questions.exp: Under the transfer-for-value rule, the exclusion is limited to the consideration paid plus subsequent premiums: $100,000 - ($20,000 + $5,000) = $75,000 taxable. Subtracting only the $20,000 purchase price forgets the premiums paid after the transfer.

questions.q: Maria, a degree candidate at a university, received a scholarship covering $15,000 of tuition, $3,000 of required books, and $6,000 of room and board. She also received $4,000 for serving as a teaching assistant, a condition of the award. How much must Maria include in gross income?
questions.exp: A qualified scholarship excludes only tuition, fees and required books and supplies; room and board ($6,000) and payments for required services ($4,000) are taxable, for $10,000. Adding the $3,000 for required books to income is the common trap.

questions.q: During the year Ken received $1,000 of interest on City of Chicago general obligation bonds, $800 of interest on U.S. Treasury bonds, $500 of interest on a federal income tax refund, and $300 of interest on a credit union savings account. What amount of interest is included in Ken's federal gross income?
questions.exp: Only state and local bond interest is excluded under §103; Treasury interest, interest on a tax refund and credit union interest are taxable: $800 + $500 + $300 = $1,600. Excluding Treasury interest confuses the state-level exemption with the federal rule.

questions.q: Rosa, a single taxpayer, has adjusted gross income of $20,000 before considering Social Security, $2,000 of tax-exempt interest, and $12,000 of Social Security benefits. Assume the base amount is $25,000 and the adjusted base amount is $34,000. How much of Rosa's Social Security benefits is taxable?
questions.exp: Provisional income is $20,000 + $2,000 + 50% of $12,000 = $28,000, which is $3,000 over the base amount; taxable benefits are the lesser of 50% x $3,000 = $1,500 or 50% of benefits ($6,000). Ignoring the 50% factor gives $3,000.

questions.q: Dana, age 45, is covered by $150,000 of employer-provided group-term life insurance. Assume the IRS Table I cost for her age is $0.15 per $1,000 of coverage per month, and Dana pays nothing toward the coverage. How much must Dana include in gross income for the year?
questions.exp: Only the cost of coverage over $50,000 is taxable under §79: ($150,000 - $50,000) / $1,000 x $0.15 x 12 = $180. Computing the cost on the full $150,000 gives $270.

questions.q: During the year Hal inherited stock worth $50,000, later received $2,000 of dividends on that stock, received a $10,000 cash gift from his aunt, and won a $1,500 raffle prize. What is Hal's gross income from these items?
questions.exp: Gifts and inheritances are excluded under §102, but income later earned on inherited property (the $2,000 dividends) and prizes ($1,500) are taxable, for $3,500. Including the cash gift treats a gift as income to the donee.

questions.q: Tom received $8,000 of state unemployment compensation, $12,000 of workers' compensation, $40,000 of compensatory damages for a physical injury suffered in a car accident, and $25,000 of punitive damages from the same lawsuit. What amount is included in Tom's gross income?
questions.exp: Unemployment compensation and punitive damages are taxable ($8,000 + $25,000 = $33,000); workers' compensation and compensatory damages for physical injury are excluded under §104. Treating punitive damages as part of the excluded injury award gives $8,000.

questions.q: Lina, a cash-basis consultant, received a $5,000 client check on December 28, Year 1, which she deposited on January 4, Year 2. She billed a client $3,000 in December, Year 1, and was paid January 10, Year 2. On December 15, Year 1, she received $2,000 of advance rent for January, Year 2, on office space she subleases. What is Lina's Year 1 gross income from these items?
questions.exp: A cash-basis taxpayer reports income when actually or constructively received: the $5,000 check (received in Year 1) plus the $2,000 advance rent (taxable when received) = $7,000. The $3,000 billed but unpaid is not Year 1 income for a cash-basis taxpayer.

questions.q: A landlord signed a one-year lease beginning December 1, Year 1, and in December received the first month's rent of $1,500, the last month's rent of $1,500, and a $1,500 security deposit refundable at the end of the lease if the tenant complies with all terms. How much rental income must the landlord report for Year 1?
questions.exp: Advance rent, including last month's rent, is income when received, but a refundable security deposit is not income while the landlord may have to return it: $1,500 + $1,500 = $3,000. Reporting only the first month's rent ignores the advance-rent rule.

questions.q: During the year Olivia's employer paid $9,000 of her health insurance premiums, contributed $5,000 to her 401(k) account, gave her a $400 holiday gift card redeemable at a grocery chain, and let her use an on-premises gym at no charge. How much of these benefits must Olivia include in gross income?
questions.exp: Employer health premiums (§106), qualified plan contributions and on-premises athletic facilities are excluded, but a gift card is a cash equivalent that can never be a de minimis fringe, so $400 is taxable. Treating the gift card as de minimis gives $0.

questions.q: A lender canceled $30,000 of Ben's personal credit card debt. Immediately before the cancellation, Ben's liabilities totaled $100,000 and the fair market value of his assets was $80,000. Ben is not in bankruptcy. How much cancellation-of-debt income must Ben include in gross income?
questions.exp: Under §108 the insolvency exclusion is limited to the amount of insolvency ($100,000 - $80,000 = $20,000), so $30,000 - $20,000 = $10,000 is taxable. Excluding the entire amount treats insolvency like a bankruptcy discharge.

questions.q: Ivy, a single taxpayer, bought and moved into a home that she used as her principal residence. After 18 months her employer transferred her to a city 400 miles away, and she sold the home at a $200,000 gain. She has never excluded gain on another home. How much of the gain must Ivy recognize?
questions.exp: A change in place of employment allows a reduced §121 exclusion: $250,000 x 18/24 = $187,500, so $200,000 - $187,500 = $12,500 is recognized. Taxing the full gain ignores the reduced-exclusion rule for unforeseen moves.

questions.q: Earl paid $60,000 for an annuity contract that pays him $500 per month for life, beginning January 1 of the current year. His expected return under the contract is $96,000. How much of the $6,000 received this year is included in Earl's gross income?
questions.exp: The exclusion ratio is $60,000 / $96,000 = 62.5%, so $3,750 of the $6,000 is a return of investment and $2,250 is taxable. The $3,750 figure is the excluded portion, not the taxable portion.

questions.q: Gina, who is not engaged in a trade or business, earned $6,000 from selling her handmade pottery as a hobby and incurred $4,000 of related expenses. How are these amounts treated on her individual return?
choices: $6,000 of gross income and a $4,000 itemized deduction
$0, because hobby income is excluded from gross income
$6,000 of gross income; the $4,000 of expenses is not deductible
$2,000 of gross income, the net hobby profit
questions.exp: Hobby receipts are fully included in gross income, while hobby expenses (formerly miscellaneous itemized deductions) are no longer deductible. Netting expenses against receipts treats the activity as a business, which it is not.

questions.q: Which of the following is excluded from an individual's gross income?
choices: Gambling winnings from a casino
The value of cash found in a used piano the taxpayer bought
Premiums paid by an employer on an employee's accident and health insurance
Fees received for serving on a jury
questions.exp: §106 excludes employer-provided accident and health coverage. Jury fees, treasure trove and gambling winnings are all items of gross income under the all-inclusive definition of §61.

questions.q: Sam owns stock with a basis of $600 in a corporation that has no current or accumulated earnings and profits. The corporation distributes $1,000 cash to Sam. How should Sam treat the distribution?
choices: $600 nontaxable return of capital and $400 capital gain
$1,000 nontaxable return of capital, leaving a negative stock basis
$600 return of capital and $400 dividend income
$1,000 dividend income
questions.exp: Without E&P there is no dividend; under §301 the distribution first reduces stock basis to zero ($600) and the $400 excess is capital gain. Basis cannot go below zero, so the excess cannot be a further return of capital.

questions.q: Nora works for a department store whose gross profit percentage on merchandise is 30%. She bought merchandise with a retail price of $1,000 for $600 under the store's employee discount program, which is available to all employees. How much must Nora include in gross income?
questions.exp: A qualified employee discount on merchandise is excluded only up to the employer's gross profit percentage: 30% x $1,000 = $300. The discount received was $400, so $100 is taxable.

questions.q: Felix's employer paid $8,000 of tuition for Felix's MBA program under a written educational assistance plan. The courses are not job-related enough to qualify as a working condition fringe. Assume the annual educational assistance exclusion is $5,250. How much must Felix include in gross income?
questions.exp: Under §127, the plan exclusion is capped at $5,250, so $8,000 - $5,250 = $2,750 is taxable. The $5,250 is the excluded amount, not the taxable amount.

questions.q: For 20 years of service, Wes received a watch with a fair market value and employer cost of $600 as an employee achievement award. The award is not under a qualified plan, and the employer's deduction for it is limited to $400. How much must Wes include in gross income?
questions.exp: Under §74 and §274, a length-of-service award of tangible property is excluded to the extent of the employer's deductible amount ($400), so the $200 excess is taxable. Treating the entire award as excluded ignores the cap.

questions.q: Ray has a traditional IRA to which he made $20,000 of nondeductible contributions over the years; he has no other IRAs. During the year he withdrew $20,000, and the IRA's value at year-end was $80,000. How much of the distribution is taxable?
questions.exp: Basis is recovered pro rata: $20,000 / ($80,000 + $20,000) = 20% nontaxable, so $4,000 is tax-free and $16,000 is taxable. Treating the withdrawal as a return of nondeductible contributions first gives $0.

questions.q: Last year Carla itemized deductions totaling $16,000, including $6,000 of state income taxes. Her standard deduction would have been $14,600. This year she received a $2,000 refund of last year's state income taxes. How much of the refund is included in Carla's gross income this year?
questions.exp: Under the tax benefit rule, the refund is taxable only to the extent the prior deduction reduced tax: itemized deductions exceeded the standard deduction by $16,000 - $14,600 = $1,400. Including the whole $2,000 ignores that $600 of the deduction gave no benefit.

questions.q: Hugo owns a lake cabin that he used personally for 60 days this year. He rented it to others for 12 days, receiving $6,000 of rent, and incurred $900 of expenses allocable to the rental days. How is the rental activity treated?
choices: $5,100 of net rental income
No rental income is reported and no rental expenses are deducted
$6,000 of income and a $900 rental deduction
$6,000 of income with no deduction for rental expenses
questions.exp: Under §280A, if a dwelling used as a residence is rented for fewer than 15 days, the rental income is excluded and rental expenses are not deductible. Reporting net rental income applies the ordinary rental rules that this de minimis rule overrides.

questions.q: Xavier, a U.S. citizen, was a bona fide resident of Germany for the entire year and earned a salary of $150,000 there. Assume the foreign earned income exclusion for the year is $130,000 and Xavier has no housing costs above the base amount. How much of his salary is included in gross income?
questions.exp: Under §911 Xavier can exclude up to $130,000 of foreign earned income, leaving $150,000 - $130,000 = $20,000 taxable. The $130,000 figure is the excluded amount, not the taxable amount.

questions.q: After an injury, Joy received $10,000 from a disability policy whose premiums were paid by her employer (and excluded from her income) and $6,000 from a disability policy she bought with her own after-tax dollars. How much of the $16,000 is included in Joy's gross income?
questions.exp: Benefits from employer-paid coverage are taxable because the premiums were never taxed, while benefits from a policy bought with after-tax dollars are excluded under §104. Reversing the two policies gives $6,000.

questions.q: As a year-end bonus, Sara's employer transferred to her 100 unrestricted shares of the employer's common stock, which had a fair market value of $40 per share. Sara paid nothing for the shares. What are Sara's gross income and her basis in the shares?
choices: $4,000 income; $4,000 basis
$0 income; $0 basis
$0 income; $4,000 basis
$4,000 income; $0 basis
questions.exp: Property received as compensation is income at its fair market value ($4,000), and the amount included becomes the tax basis, so later gain is not taxed twice. A zero basis would double-tax the $4,000.

questions.q: Under a divorce agreement executed in 2016 and never modified, Leo pays his former spouse $2,000 per month, decreasing to $1,500 per month when their child reaches age 18. The child is 12. How much of the $24,000 paid this year must the former spouse include in gross income?
questions.exp: Pre-2019 instruments keep the old rule that alimony is taxable to the recipient, but a reduction tied to a child contingency is treated as child support: $500 x 12 = $6,000 is child support, leaving $18,000 of alimony. Applying the post-2018 rule gives $0.

questions.q: Alma was selected, without any application or action on her part, to receive a $50,000 literary achievement award. She is not required to perform future services, and before receiving any funds she directed the payor to transfer the entire award to a qualified charity. How much must Alma include in gross income?
choices: $25,000, because half of a literary award is excluded
$0, because the award is excluded when transferred to a designated charity
$50,000, offset by a $50,000 charitable contribution deduction
$50,000, with no deduction allowed
questions.exp: §74 excludes an award for literary, scientific, artistic or civic achievement if the recipient was selected without action, need not perform services, and has the payor transfer it to a charity. Including the award and taking a contribution deduction would not produce the same result because of AGI limits and itemizing.

questions.q: Ted settled an age discrimination claim against his former employer, receiving $40,000 of back pay and $10,000 for emotional distress. Ted suffered no physical injury or physical sickness and paid no medical expenses for the emotional distress. How much of the settlement is included in Ted's gross income?
questions.exp: §104 excludes damages only for personal physical injury or physical sickness; back pay and emotional distress damages not attributable to a physical injury are fully taxable ($50,000). Excluding the emotional distress portion is the trap.

questions.q: Ari exchanged investment land with an adjusted basis of $40,000 and a fair market value of $100,000 for other investment land worth $90,000 plus $10,000 cash. What gain does Ari recognize?
questions.exp: Realized gain is $100,000 - $40,000 = $60,000, but under §1031 gain is recognized only to the extent of boot received ($10,000). Recognizing the full realized gain ignores the like-kind deferral.

questions.q: Bea exchanged a rental building with an adjusted basis of $150,000 and a fair market value of $200,000 for another rental building worth $180,000 plus $20,000 cash. What is Bea's basis in the building she received?
questions.exp: Basis is the old basis plus gain recognized ($20,000) minus boot received ($20,000): $150,000; equivalently, $180,000 value less $30,000 deferred gain. Subtracting the boot without adding the recognized gain gives $130,000.

questions.q: Cy exchanged an office building (adjusted basis $300,000, fair market value $500,000, subject to a $100,000 mortgage that the other party assumed) for a warehouse worth $400,000 with no mortgage. Both properties are held for business use. What gain does Cy recognize?
questions.exp: Relief from a liability is treated as boot received; realized gain is $400,000 + $100,000 - $300,000 = $200,000, and recognized gain is limited to the $100,000 of boot. Ignoring liability relief gives $0.

questions.q: Dee exchanged business real estate worth $500,000 (basis $200,000, subject to a $100,000 mortgage assumed by the other party) for real estate worth $470,000 subject to a $60,000 mortgage that Dee assumed. Dee also paid $10,000 cash. What gain does Dee recognize?
questions.exp: Liabilities are netted: net relief of $100,000 - $60,000 = $40,000 is boot received, which is offset by the $10,000 cash Dee paid, so recognized gain is $30,000. Ignoring the cash paid gives $40,000.

questions.q: Which of the following exchanges qualifies for nonrecognition under §1031?
choices: An interest in one partnership for an interest in another partnership
An apartment building for unimproved land held for investment
A business truck for another business truck
U.S. land for land located in France
questions.exp: Since 2018, §1031 applies only to real property held for business or investment, and improved and unimproved U.S. real estate are like-kind. Personal property such as trucks, foreign real property and partnership interests do not qualify.

questions.q: Eve exchanged investment land with her brother in a valid like-kind exchange and deferred a $50,000 gain. Eighteen months later her brother sold the land he received from Eve to an unrelated buyer. What is the tax consequence to Eve?
choices: Only Eve's brother recognizes gain
Eve recognizes the $50,000 deferred gain in the year of her brother's sale
Eve must amend her return for the year of the exchange to recognize the gain
There is no consequence to Eve because the exchange was completed
questions.exp: Under the related-party rule, if either party disposes of the exchanged property within two years, the deferred gain is recognized as of the date of that disposition, so Eve reports it in the year of the sale. No amended return is required.

questions.q: On March 1, Fay transferred investment real estate to a qualified intermediary to begin a deferred like-kind exchange. Which deadlines must she meet?
choices: Identify replacement property within 45 days and receive it within 180 days after identification
Identify and receive replacement property within 180 days, with no separate identification deadline
Identify replacement property within 45 days of the transfer and receive it within 180 days of the transfer or by the due date of her return (with extensions), if earlier
Identify replacement property within 60 days and receive it within one year
questions.exp: Both deadlines run from the transfer of the relinquished property: 45 days to identify and the earlier of 180 days or the return due date (including extensions) to receive. Counting the 180 days from identification is the trap.

questions.q: Gus's warehouse had declined in value to $80,000, well below its $100,000 adjusted basis. In a qualifying §1031 transaction he swapped it for a smaller business building valued at $70,000 and also received $10,000 cash. What basis does Gus take in the smaller building?
questions.exp: The $20,000 realized loss is not recognized, even with boot; basis is $100,000 old basis - $10,000 boot + $0 gain = $90,000. Using fair market value of $70,000 would allow the unrecognized loss to disappear.

questions.q: Hal exchanged investment land (basis $50,000, value $80,000) plus stock held for investment (basis $30,000, value $20,000) for investment land worth $100,000. What gain or loss does Hal recognize?
questions.exp: Non-like-kind property given as boot is treated as sold, so Hal recognizes the $10,000 loss on the stock, while the $30,000 gain on the land is deferred because he received no boot. Treating the whole transaction as nontaxable gives $0.

questions.q: Ida held investment land for four years and exchanged it in a valid like-kind exchange for other investment land, receiving no boot. Five months later she sold the new land at a gain. What is the character of the gain?
choices: Ordinary income, because the exchange occurred within one year
Long-term, because the holding period of the land given up tacks on
Short-term, unless she received boot in the exchange
Short-term, because the new land was held five months
questions.exp: Property received in a like-kind exchange takes a substituted basis and includes the holding period of the property given up, so the gain is long-term. Starting a new holding period applies only to boot property.

questions.q: The state condemned Jack's business building, which had an adjusted basis of $300,000, and paid him $500,000. Within the replacement period he bought a similar building for $450,000 and elected to defer gain. What gain does Jack recognize?
questions.exp: Under §1033, gain is recognized to the extent the proceeds are not reinvested: $500,000 - $450,000 = $50,000, and the remaining $150,000 is deferred. The $150,000 figure is the deferred gain, not the recognized gain.

questions.q: Fire destroyed Kim's rental building, which had an adjusted basis of $120,000. She received $200,000 of insurance and within the replacement period bought a similar rental building for $230,000, electing to defer gain. What is her basis in the new building?
questions.exp: All $80,000 of realized gain is deferred because she reinvested more than the proceeds, so her basis is the $230,000 cost less the $80,000 deferred gain, or $150,000. Using the full cost ignores the deferral.

questions.q: A city condemned real property that Lee held for investment, and Lee realized a gain when he received the award. Within what period must Lee acquire replacement property to defer the gain?
choices: 180 days after the condemnation
Two years after the close of the first tax year in which any part of the gain is realized
One year after the condemnation award
Three years after the close of the first tax year in which any part of the gain is realized
questions.exp: For condemned real property held for business or investment, the replacement period is three years after the close of the first tax year in which gain is realized. The general two-year period applies to other involuntary conversions, such as casualties of personal property.

questions.q: The state condemned Mo's warehouse used in his business, and he reinvested the entire award in unimproved land that he holds for investment. Does the replacement qualify for deferral under §1033?
choices: Yes, but only if the replacement occurs within 180 days
No, because raw land is not depreciable
No, because replacement property must be similar or related in service or use
Yes, because condemned business or investment real property may be replaced with like-kind real property
questions.exp: For condemnations of real property held for business or investment, §1033 allows replacement with like-kind property, a broader standard than similar or related in service or use. The narrower standard applies to casualties and to other types of property.

questions.q: Which statement about nonrecognition of gain under §1033 is correct?
choices: Nonrecognition is mandatory when property is converted directly into similar property, but elective when the taxpayer receives money and reinvests it
Nonrecognition is elective in all cases
Nonrecognition is available only when property is converted directly into similar property
Nonrecognition is mandatory in all cases
questions.exp: A direct conversion into similar property requires nonrecognition, while a conversion into money allows the taxpayer to elect deferral if qualified replacement property is bought. Most conversions are into cash, so treating the rule as always mandatory is wrong.

questions.q: Nan, single, lived in her principal residence for ten years. Fire destroyed it; her basis was $200,000 and she received $600,000 of insurance. She qualifies for the $250,000 §121 exclusion and, within the replacement period, built a new residence for $300,000, electing §1033 deferral. What gain does Nan recognize?
questions.exp: Of the $400,000 realized gain, $250,000 is excluded under §121; for §1033 the amount realized is reduced by the excluded gain to $350,000, so failing to reinvest $50,000 makes $50,000 recognized. Ignoring §1033 gives $150,000.

questions.q: Opal exchanged investment land (basis $60,000, value $100,000) for other investment land worth $90,000 plus $10,000 cash. She paid a $2,000 broker commission on the exchange. What gain does Opal recognize?
questions.exp: Exchange expenses paid reduce the cash boot received: $10,000 - $2,000 = $8,000 recognized, out of a realized gain of $100,000 - $2,000 - $60,000 = $38,000. Ignoring the commission gives $10,000.

questions.q: In a deferred like-kind exchange, which identification of replacement property is valid without regard to the fair market values of the properties identified?
choices: Any number of potential replacement properties
Up to three potential replacement properties
Up to five potential replacement properties
Only one replacement property
questions.exp: Under the three-property rule, a taxpayer may identify up to three properties regardless of value; identifying more requires satisfying the 200% or 95% value tests. Identifying any number without limit is not permitted.

questions.q: Pam traded her old business truck (adjusted basis $10,000, fair market value $18,000) plus $30,000 cash to a dealer for a new business truck worth $48,000. What is her basis in the new truck?
questions.exp: Since 2018 §1031 applies only to real property, so the trade is taxable: Pam recognizes $8,000 of gain and takes a cost basis of $48,000. The $40,000 carryover-plus-cash basis applies the repealed personal-property rule.

questions.q: On March 15, Year 1, a fire destroyed Quinn's business equipment (not real property). He received insurance proceeds and realized a gain in Year 1. What is the last day he may buy replacement equipment and still elect deferral under §1033?
choices: March 15, Year 3
December 31, Year 3
December 31, Year 2
December 31, Year 4
questions.exp: The general replacement period ends two years after the close of the first tax year in which any part of the gain is realized: December 31, Year 3. Measuring two years from the date of the fire gives March 15, Year 3.

questions.q: Rae exchanged investment land with an adjusted basis of $95,000 and a fair market value of $100,000 for investment land worth $80,000 plus $20,000 cash. What gain does Rae recognize, and what is her basis in the land received?
questions.exp: Recognized gain is the lesser of realized gain ($5,000) or boot ($20,000); basis is $95,000 + $5,000 - $20,000 = $80,000. Recognizing the full boot ignores the cap at realized gain.

questions.q: Sid exchanged investment land with a basis of $50,000 and a value of $80,000, plus $20,000 cash, for investment land worth $100,000. What is Sid's basis in the new land?
questions.exp: Boot paid does not trigger gain, and it is added to basis: $50,000 + $20,000 = $70,000, which preserves the $30,000 deferred gain. Using the new land's $100,000 value would eliminate the deferred gain.

questions.q: Tia exchanged investment real estate worth $100,000 with an adjusted basis of $120,000 for other investment real estate worth $100,000. She would like to deduct her loss. Which statement is correct?
choices: Nonrecognition is mandatory, so the realized loss cannot be deducted and is preserved in the basis of the new property
Nonrecognition applies only to gains, so the loss is deductible
Nonrecognition is elective, so Tia may choose to deduct the $20,000 loss
The loss is deductible only to the extent of boot received
questions.exp: §1031 is not elective: when its requirements are met, neither gain nor loss is recognized, and the $120,000 basis carries over to preserve the loss. To deduct the loss, Tia would have to sell the property in a taxable sale instead.

questions.q: After the city announced it would condemn his rental property for a road project, Uri sold the property to the city before formal condemnation proceedings began and realized a gain. May Uri elect §1033 deferral if he reinvests the proceeds?
choices: Yes, because a sale under threat or imminence of condemnation is treated as an involuntary conversion
No, because he received cash rather than property
Yes, but only if he reinvests within 180 days
No, because no formal condemnation proceeding was begun
