questions.exp: §1033 covers sales made under threat or imminence of condemnation, not only formal takings. Receiving cash is the usual case and allows the deferral election when replacement property is bought.

questions.q: Val exchanged business real estate worth $300,000 (basis $100,000, subject to a $50,000 mortgage assumed by the other party) for real estate worth $380,000 subject to a $130,000 mortgage that Val assumed. What is Val's basis in the property received?
questions.exp: Val assumed more debt than he was relieved of, so he received no net boot and recognizes no gain; basis is $100,000 + $130,000 liability assumed - $50,000 liability relieved = $180,000. Ignoring the liabilities gives $100,000.

questions.q: The state condemned land that Wes held for investment, which had a basis of $200,000, and paid him $150,000. Wes reinvested the entire award in similar land. How is the $50,000 realized loss treated?
choices: Only $25,000 is recognized
It is deferred until the replacement land is sold
It is deferred into the basis of the replacement land
It is recognized as a $50,000 loss
questions.exp: §1033 defers only gains; a loss from an involuntary conversion of business or investment property is recognized regardless of reinvestment. Treating §1033 like §1031 would wrongly defer the loss.

questions.q: Fire destroyed Xia's business building, which had an adjusted basis of $250,000. She received $400,000 of insurance, used $100,000 of it to pay off the building's mortgage, and reinvested $300,000 in a replacement building within the replacement period, electing deferral. What gain does Xia recognize?
questions.exp: Gain is recognized to the extent proceeds are not reinvested in replacement property: $400,000 - $300,000 = $100,000. Using proceeds to pay off a mortgage is not reinvestment, so assuming full deferral is wrong.

questions.q: Yuki exchanged investment land with a basis of $120,000 and a value of $300,000 for two parcels of investment land worth $200,000 and $100,000, receiving no boot. What is her basis in the $200,000 parcel?
questions.exp: The $120,000 substituted basis is allocated by relative fair market values: $120,000 x $200,000 / $300,000 = $80,000. Using the parcel's fair market value would eliminate the deferred gain.

questions.q: Zack agreed to exchange his investment land for other investment land. At closing, the buyer paid the sale proceeds directly to Zack, who deposited them and used them 30 days later to buy replacement land from a different seller. How is the transaction treated?
choices: As a taxable sale, because Zack actually received the cash proceeds
As a deferred exchange to the extent the proceeds were reinvested
As a valid deferred exchange, because replacement occurred within 45 days
As a valid exchange if the replacement land is of equal or greater value
questions.exp: Actual or constructive receipt of the proceeds before acquiring replacement property makes the transaction a taxable sale; a qualified intermediary must hold the funds. Meeting the 45-day deadline does not cure receipt of the cash.

questions.q: A real estate developer exchanged several subdivided lots it held for sale to customers for an apartment building that it will hold as a rental investment. Does the exchange qualify under §1031?
choices: Yes, but only if both parties are dealers
No, because property held primarily for sale is excluded from §1031
Yes, because both properties are real property
Yes, but only if no boot is received
questions.exp: §1031 requires that the property given up be held for productive use in a business or for investment; real estate held primarily for sale (dealer property) does not qualify. Being real property alone is not enough.

questions.q: A promissory note is otherwise in proper form. Which additional term would cause the note to be nonnegotiable under UCC Article 3?
choices: 'This note is secured by a mortgage dated June 1'
'Payable on demand'
'This note is subject to the terms of the purchase agreement between the maker and the payee dated June 1'
'Interest is payable at the payee bank's prime rate, as it varies from time to time'
questions.exp: A promise expressly subject to or governed by another writing is conditional and not negotiable (UCC 3-106). A mere reference to collateral or a variable interest rate does not destroy negotiability.

questions.q: Mae signed a writing stating, 'I promise to pay Ann Lee $1,000 on December 1, Year 2,' with no other terms. Which statement is correct?
choices: It is not a negotiable instrument because it is not payable to order or to bearer
It is a negotiable draft
It is a negotiable note because it is a written, unconditional promise to pay a fixed amount at a definite time
It is negotiable only if Ann Lee indorses it
questions.exp: To be negotiable under UCC 3-104, a note must contain words of negotiability, payable 'to the order of' or 'to bearer'; 'pay Ann Lee' lacks them. Only checks are excepted from the order-or-bearer requirement.

questions.q: Which person is most likely a holder in due course of a properly negotiated note?
choices: Dee, who bought the note two weeks after its due date
Gus, who promised to pay the payee for the note next month and has not yet paid
Fay, who paid the payee 90% of the note's face value before maturity, in good faith and without notice of any defense
Eli, who received the note as a birthday gift from the payee
questions.exp: A holder in due course must take for value, in good faith and without notice that the instrument is overdue or subject to defenses (UCC 3-302); buying at a reasonable discount is still value. A gift is not value, an executory promise is not value until performed, and an overdue instrument gives notice.

questions.q: Hal holds a note as a holder in due course. When Hal demanded payment, the maker raised several defenses. Which defense is effective against Hal?
choices: The payee breached the underlying contract
The maker was a minor when she signed the note, and state law makes minors' contracts voidable
The payee fraudulently induced the maker to sign the note by lying about the quality of goods
The goods for which the note was given were never delivered
questions.exp: Real defenses such as infancy (to the extent it is a defense to a simple contract), fraud in the execution, forgery, bankruptcy discharge and illegality that voids the obligation are good against a holder in due course (UCC 3-305). Fraud in the inducement, failure of consideration and breach of contract are personal defenses cut off by HDC status.

questions.q: Ivy signed a $1,000 note payable to the order of Jack. Jack fraudulently raised the amount to $10,000 and negotiated the note to Kim, a holder in due course who could not detect the alteration. How much can Kim recover from Ivy?
choices: $0, because the note was materially altered
questions.exp: A fraudulent material alteration discharges the maker except against a holder in due course, who may enforce the instrument according to its original terms (UCC 3-407). Kim therefore recovers the original $1,000.

questions.q: Lou, a holder in due course of a note, gave the note to his niece, Mia, as a gift. The maker has a personal defense of failure of consideration against the original payee. Mia knew of the defense when she received the note. Can Mia enforce the note against the maker?
choices: Yes, because Mia acquired Lou's rights as a holder in due course under the shelter rule
No, because Mia did not give value
Yes, but only to the extent of the value Lou paid
No, because Mia knew of the defense
questions.exp: Under the shelter rule (UCC 3-203), a transferee acquires the transferor's rights, including HDC rights, even without value or with notice, unless the transferee participated in fraud or illegality affecting the instrument. Mia was not a party to any wrongdoing.

questions.q: Nell received a check payable to her order and signed only her name on the back. She then lost the check. Oz found it and sold it to Pat, who paid value in good faith without notice of the loss. Which statement is correct?
choices: Pat is a holder only if Oz also indorsed the check
Pat can be a holder in due course because the blank indorsement made the check bearer paper, negotiable by delivery alone
Pat cannot be a holder because Oz's indorsement was missing
Pat took subject to Nell's claim because the check was lost
questions.exp: A blank indorsement (signature alone) converts order paper to bearer paper, which is negotiated by delivery alone (UCC 3-205), so Pat is a holder and can qualify as an HDC. A special indorsement would have prevented this result.

questions.q: Quinn indorsed a note 'Without recourse, Quinn' and transferred it for value to Rose. The maker later refused to pay because of insolvency, of which Quinn had no knowledge. Which statement is correct?
choices: Quinn is liable because she warranted that the maker would pay
Quinn is liable to Rose on her indorser's contract
Quinn is not liable on her indorsement contract, but she still makes transfer warranties
Quinn's qualified indorsement made the note nonnegotiable
questions.exp: A qualified ('without recourse') indorsement disclaims the indorser's secondary contract liability for payment (UCC 3-415) but does not eliminate transfer warranties, which do not include a guarantee of the maker's solvency. It does not affect negotiability.

questions.q: Ruth indorsed a note in blank and negotiated it to Sam. At maturity Sam presented the note to the maker, who dishonored it. To hold Ruth liable as an unqualified indorser, what must Sam generally do?
choices: Give Ruth timely notice of dishonor
Sue the maker first and obtain an unsatisfied judgment
Have the note formally protested by a notary in all cases
Nothing further, because indorsers are primarily liable
questions.exp: An indorser is secondarily liable; the obligation arises only after presentment and dishonor, and the indorser is discharged if timely notice of dishonor is not given (UCC 3-503). Protest is required only for certain international drafts.

questions.q: A person who transfers a negotiable instrument for consideration makes several warranties to the transferee. Which of the following is NOT one of those transfer warranties?
choices: The instrument has not been altered
All signatures on the instrument are authentic and authorized
The transferor is entitled to enforce the instrument
The maker or drawer is solvent and will pay the instrument
questions.exp: Transfer warranties under UCC 3-416 include entitlement to enforce, authentic signatures, no alteration, no defenses good against the transferor, and no knowledge of insolvency proceedings against the obligor. A transferor does not warrant that the obligor is solvent or will pay.

questions.q: An imposter, falsely claiming to be Tom Ward, persuaded Vale Co. to issue a check payable to 'Tom Ward.' The imposter indorsed the check 'Tom Ward' and cashed it at a bank, which collected from Vale's bank. Who generally bears the loss?
choices: The cashing bank, because it took from a forger
The real Tom Ward
Vale Co., because the imposter's indorsement is effective under the imposter rule
Vale's bank, because it paid on a forged indorsement
questions.exp: Under the imposter rule (UCC 3-404), an indorsement in the payee's name by the imposter is effective in favor of a person who pays or takes the instrument in good faith, so the drawer that was deceived bears the loss (subject to comparative negligence). The usual rule that a forged indorsement is ineffective does not apply.

questions.q: On May 1, Walt orally ordered his bank to stop payment on a check he had written. He never confirmed the order in writing. On May 20 the check was presented, and the bank paid it. Which statement is correct?
choices: The bank is liable because oral stop-payment orders are effective until revoked
The bank is not liable because an oral stop-payment order lapses after 14 days unless confirmed in writing
The bank is liable because it must honor any stop-payment order
The bank is liable because a stop-payment order is effective for six months
questions.exp: Under UCC 4-403, an oral stop-payment order is binding for only 14 days unless confirmed in writing within that time; a written order is effective for six months and may be renewed. The bank paid after the oral order lapsed.

questions.q: A customer's ordinary check was presented to the drawee bank eight months after its date. The customer had not issued a stop-payment order, and the bank paid the check in good faith. Is the bank liable to the customer?
choices: No, because checks never become stale
Yes, unless the customer confirmed the check in writing
No, because a bank may, but is not obligated to, pay a stale check in good faith
Yes, because banks may not pay checks presented more than six months after their date
questions.exp: Under UCC 4-404, a bank has no obligation to pay an uncertified check presented more than six months after its date, but it may pay in good faith and charge the customer's account. Staleness permits, but does not require, dishonor.

questions.q: A consumer bought a defective refrigerator from a dealer and signed an installment note, which the dealer sold to a finance company that otherwise qualifies as a holder in due course. Under the FTC holder-in-due-course rule, which statement is correct?
choices: The consumer may assert defenses only if the finance company knew of the defect
The note is void
The consumer may assert claims and defenses against the seller against the finance company
The finance company takes free of the consumer's defenses
questions.exp: The FTC rule requires consumer credit contracts to contain a notice preserving the consumer's claims and defenses against any holder, effectively eliminating HDC protection in consumer credit sales. The finance company's knowledge is irrelevant.

questions.q: On March 1, Ace Supply, a merchant, gave Bolt Co. a signed written offer to sell 500 valves at $20 each, stating the offer would remain open for 60 days. Bolt gave no consideration. On March 20, Ace revoked. On April 10, Bolt accepted. Is there a contract?
choices: No, because Bolt gave no consideration to keep the offer open
Yes, because Ace's signed written offer was an irrevocable firm offer for the stated period
Yes, but only if Bolt is also a merchant
No, because Ace revoked before acceptance
questions.exp: Under UCC 2-205, a merchant's signed written offer that gives assurance it will be held open is irrevocable without consideration for the time stated, up to three months. Only the offeror must be a merchant.

questions.q: Cobb Co. sent Dart Co. a signed offer to sell goods, stating: 'Acceptance is expressly limited to the terms of this offer.' Dart, a merchant, replied with a definite acceptance that added a term requiring Cobb to pay freight. Which statement is correct?
choices: A contract was formed on Cobb's terms, and the freight term is not part of it
A contract was formed, and the freight term is included unless Cobb objects within 10 days
A contract was formed, and the freight term is included because both parties are merchants
There is no contract, because the acceptance added a term
questions.exp: Under UCC 2-207, a definite acceptance with additional terms still forms a contract; between merchants, the additional terms become part of it unless the offer expressly limits acceptance to its terms, the terms materially alter it, or objection is given. The offer's limitation excludes the freight term.

questions.q: Fox Corp. and Gale Co., both merchants, orally agreed that Fox would buy 1,000 widgets from Gale for $8,000. The next day Gale sent Fox a signed written confirmation of the agreement. Fox received it, read it, and did not respond. A month later Fox refused to accept delivery, citing the statute of frauds. Is the contract enforceable against Fox?
choices: No, because Fox never signed a writing
Yes, because Fox did not object in writing within 10 days after receiving the confirmation
Yes, but only up to $500
No, because the contract was for more than $500
questions.exp: Under the merchant confirmation rule of UCC 2-201, a written confirmation sufficient against the sender binds a merchant recipient who has reason to know its contents and fails to object in writing within 10 days. Fox's lack of signature does not matter.

questions.q: Hoyt orally ordered 200 signs printed with his store's logo for $5,000 from Ink Co. The signs were not suitable for sale to others. After Ink had substantially completed production, Hoyt repudiated, citing the statute of frauds. Is the contract enforceable?
choices: No, unless Hoyt admits the contract in court
Yes, because the goods were specially manufactured and the seller substantially began performance before repudiation
No, because a contract for goods of $500 or more must be in writing
Yes, but only for $500
questions.exp: UCC 2-201 makes an oral contract enforceable for specially manufactured goods not suitable for sale to others if the seller has made a substantial beginning before notice of repudiation. Admission in court is a separate exception.

questions.q: Jet Co. contracted to sell machinery to Kay Corp., 'F.O.B. Jet's warehouse.' Jet delivered conforming goods to the carrier and promptly notified Kay. The goods were destroyed in a highway accident while in transit. Who bears the risk of loss?
choices: Kay, because risk passed when conforming goods were duly delivered to the carrier under a shipment contract
The carrier, because the goods were in its possession
Jet, because Kay never received the goods
Jet and Kay equally
questions.exp: F.O.B. the seller's place of shipment creates a shipment contract; under UCC 2-509, risk passes to the buyer when the seller duly delivers conforming goods to the carrier. In a destination contract, risk would remain with the seller until tender at the destination.

questions.q: Lark, a merchant furniture dealer, sold a sofa to Moe, who paid in full and agreed to pick it up the next day. That night, without Lark's fault, a fire destroyed the sofa at Lark's store. No carrier was involved. Who bears the loss?
choices: Lark, because risk passes from a merchant seller only on the buyer's receipt of the goods
Moe, because title passed at the time of contracting
Moe, because he had paid in full
Moe and Lark equally
questions.exp: When no carrier is involved, risk passes to the buyer on receipt of the goods if the seller is a merchant, or on tender of delivery if not (UCC 2-509). Title and payment do not control risk of loss under Article 2.

questions.q: Nova Co. shipped goods to Ola Inc. under a shipment contract, but the goods did not conform to the contract specifications. The goods were destroyed in transit before Ola could inspect them. Who bears the risk of loss?
choices: The carrier only
Ola, because the contract was a shipment contract
Nova, because risk does not pass to the buyer when the seller ships nonconforming goods that the buyer may reject
Ola, because it had not yet rejected the goods
questions.exp: Under UCC 2-510, when a tender or delivery so fails to conform that the buyer has a right to reject, risk of loss remains on the seller until cure or acceptance. The ordinary shipment-contract rule assumes conforming goods.

questions.q: Pia left her watch for repair with Quill Jewelers, which also sells new and used watches. Quill mistakenly sold Pia's watch to Rob, who paid fair value and had no knowledge of Pia's ownership. Who is entitled to the watch?
choices: Pia, unless Rob paid more than fair value
Rob, only if Pia was negligent in choosing Quill
Rob, because a merchant entrusted with goods of the kind it deals in can transfer the owner's rights to a buyer in the ordinary course of business
Pia, because Quill had no title to the watch
questions.exp: Under the entrustment rule of UCC 2-403, entrusting goods to a merchant who deals in goods of that kind gives the merchant power to transfer all the entruster's rights to a buyer in the ordinary course. Pia's remedy is against Quill.

questions.q: Sal bought a painting from Tia and paid with a check that later bounced. Before Tia discovered this, Sal sold the painting to Uri, who paid fair value in good faith without notice. Can Tia recover the painting from Uri?
choices: No, because Tia was a merchant
Yes, because Sal never paid for the painting
No, because Sal had voidable title and could transfer good title to a good-faith purchaser for value
Yes, because Sal obtained the painting by fraud
questions.exp: A buyer who obtains goods with a check later dishonored acquires voidable title and can transfer good title to a good-faith purchaser for value (UCC 2-403). A thief, by contrast, has void title and can pass none.

questions.q: A used-car dealer wants to sell a car without any implied warranty of merchantability. Which of the following would most likely accomplish this?
choices: A written disclaimer of merchantability printed in fine print on the back of the contract
Selling the car with a conspicuous notation that it is sold 'as is'
An oral statement that the car carries no warranty of fitness for a particular purpose
A statement that the dealer is not bound by express statements made by its salespeople
questions.exp: Under UCC 2-316, expressions like 'as is' or 'with all faults' exclude all implied warranties; otherwise a merchantability disclaimer must mention merchantability and, if written, be conspicuous. Fitness disclaimers must be in writing, and disclaimers inconsistent with express warranties are inoperative.

questions.q: Vic, who is not a merchant, told Wren that he needed a pump capable of moving water 300 feet uphill on his farm, and relied on Wren to select one. Wren, also not a merchant, sold Vic a pump she selected, which could move water only 100 feet. Which warranty did Wren breach?
choices: The implied warranty of merchantability
The warranty of title
No warranty, because Wren is not a merchant
The implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose
questions.exp: The implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose (UCC 2-315) arises when the seller has reason to know the buyer's particular purpose and that the buyer relies on the seller's skill to select the goods; the seller need not be a merchant. Merchantability requires a merchant seller.

questions.q: Yale Co. contracted to deliver 100 blue chairs to Zed Inc. by June 30. On June 10, Yale delivered red chairs, and Zed rejected them. Yale promptly notified Zed that it would deliver conforming blue chairs by June 25. Which statement is correct?
choices: Zed may cancel the contract immediately because the tender was not perfect
Yale has the right to cure by delivering conforming goods by June 30
Yale may cure only if Zed consents
Zed must accept the red chairs at a reduced price
questions.exp: Under UCC 2-508, when a nonconforming tender is rejected and the time for performance has not expired, the seller may seasonably notify the buyer and make a conforming delivery within the contract time. The perfect tender rule is tempered by this right to cure.

questions.q: Seller breached a contract to deliver goods to Buyer for $10,000. Buyer promptly and reasonably bought substitute goods for $12,500 and incurred $300 of incidental expenses. Buyer saved no expenses because of the breach and has no consequential damages. What may Buyer recover?
questions.exp: Cover damages under UCC 2-712 are the cover price minus the contract price ($2,500) plus incidental and consequential damages ($300), less expenses saved, for a total of $2,800. Omitting incidental damages gives $2,500.

questions.q: Buyer wrongfully repudiated a contract to buy goods for $20,000. Seller resold the goods in a commercially reasonable private sale, with proper notice to Buyer, for $16,000 and incurred $500 of incidental expenses. Seller saved no expenses. What may Seller recover?
questions.exp: Under UCC 2-706, the seller may recover the contract price less the resale price ($4,000) plus incidental damages ($500), less expenses saved, or $4,500. Subtracting the incidental expenses instead of adding them gives $3,500.

questions.q: Seller shipped goods on credit to Buyer. While the goods were in transit, Seller learned that Buyer had become insolvent. What may Seller do?
choices: Stop delivery only if Buyer has filed for bankruptcy
Stop delivery of the goods in the carrier's possession and demand cash for them
Nothing, because title passed when the goods were shipped
Sue Buyer for the price immediately without stopping delivery, but not stop the goods
questions.exp: Under UCC 2-705, a seller who discovers the buyer's insolvency may stop delivery of goods in the possession of a carrier and refuse delivery except for cash. Passage of title does not prevent stoppage in transit, and a bankruptcy filing is not required.

questions.q: Ann bought a computer system from a dealer and accepted it after a brief inspection. Two months later, she discovered a latent defect that caused frequent crashes and substantially impaired the system's value to her; the dealer was unable to fix it. Which statement is correct?
choices: Ann may revoke acceptance only if the dealer agrees
Ann cannot return the system because she accepted it
Ann may revoke her acceptance within a reasonable time after discovering the defect
Ann may only sue for damages and must keep the system
questions.exp: Under UCC 2-608, a buyer may revoke acceptance of goods whose nonconformity substantially impairs their value if acceptance was reasonably induced by the difficulty of discovering the defect, and revocation occurs within a reasonable time after discovery. Acceptance does not foreclose this remedy.

questions.q: Adams contributed land with an adjusted basis of $40,000 and a fair market value of $100,000 to a partnership in exchange for a 25% interest. The land was subject to a $30,000 mortgage, which the partnership assumed. What is Adams's initial basis in the partnership interest?
questions.exp: Basis = $40,000 contributed basis − $30,000 liability relief + 25% × $30,000 share of the assumed liability = $17,500 (§§722, 752). Adding the liability share without subtracting the full relief gives $47,500.

questions.q: Baker contributed property with an adjusted basis of $20,000, a fair market value of $90,000, and subject to a $60,000 mortgage to a partnership for a 50% interest. The partnership assumed the mortgage. How much gain must Baker recognize on the contribution?
questions.exp: Basis would be $20,000 − $60,000 + $30,000 (50% share) = −$10,000; the net $30,000 liability relief exceeding basis is a deemed cash distribution, so Baker recognizes $10,000 gain and takes a $0 basis (§§731, 752). Section 721 nonrecognition does not protect liability relief in excess of basis.

questions.q: Clark received a 20% capital interest in an existing partnership in exchange for services rendered to the partnership. The interest had a fair market value of $30,000 when received. How should Clark treat the receipt of the interest?
choices: $30,000 of ordinary income, and a $30,000 basis in the interest
No income, because transfers in exchange for a partnership interest are nontaxable under §721
$30,000 of capital gain
No income until the interest is sold, at which time the gain is ordinary
questions.exp: Section 721 covers contributions of property, not services; a capital interest received for services is ordinary compensation income equal to its FMV, which also becomes the partner's basis. Treating services as 'property' under §721 is the common trap.

questions.q: Davis contributed equipment with an adjusted basis of $12,000 and a fair market value of $18,000 to a partnership. Davis had used the equipment in business for four years. What is the partnership's basis and holding period for the equipment?
choices: $12,000, with a holding period beginning on the contribution date
$18,000, with a holding period that includes Davis's holding period
$12,000, with a holding period that includes Davis's holding period
$18,000, with a holding period beginning on the contribution date
questions.exp: The partnership takes a carryover basis under §723 and, because the basis is determined by reference to the contributor's basis, the holding period tacks under §1223(2). FMV basis would apply only in a taxable exchange.

questions.q: At the beginning of the year, Evans had a $50,000 basis in a partnership interest. For the year, Evans's distributive share included $20,000 of ordinary business income, $2,000 of tax-exempt interest, and a $5,000 §179 deduction. Evans received $15,000 of cash distributions, and Evans's share of partnership liabilities increased by $8,000. What is Evans's basis at year-end?
questions.exp: $50,000 + $20,000 + $2,000 tax-exempt income − $5,000 §179 − $15,000 distributions + $8,000 liability increase = $60,000 (§705, §752). Omitting the tax-exempt interest, which does increase basis, gives $58,000.

questions.q: Before considering this year's results, Foster's basis in a partnership interest was $10,000. Foster's distributive share of the partnership's ordinary loss for the year is $16,000. How is the loss treated?
choices: Foster deducts nothing until the partnership has income
Foster deducts $16,000 and has a negative basis of $6,000
Foster deducts $10,000 and the remaining $6,000 is permanently lost
Foster deducts $10,000 and carries forward $6,000 indefinitely until basis is restored
questions.exp: Under §704 a partner's loss deduction is limited to outside basis; the $6,000 excess is suspended and carried forward indefinitely until basis increases. Basis can never go below zero.

questions.q: Green's basis in a partnership interest was $30,000. In a nonliquidating distribution, Green received $10,000 cash and land with a partnership adjusted basis of $25,000 and a fair market value of $40,000. What is Green's basis in the land?
questions.exp: Cash reduces basis first to $20,000; in a nonliquidating distribution the property's basis is the partnership's basis ($25,000) limited to the partner's remaining outside basis, or $20,000 (§732). No gain is recognized because only cash in excess of basis triggers gain.

questions.q: Hill's basis in a partnership interest was $12,000. Hill received a nonliquidating cash distribution of $15,000. The partnership holds no unrealized receivables or inventory. What is the tax result to Hill?
choices: $15,000 of capital gain
$3,000 of ordinary income
$3,000 of capital gain
No gain; basis is reduced to $0 and $3,000 is carried forward
questions.exp: Money distributed in excess of outside basis produces gain under §731, treated as gain from sale of the partnership interest (capital), so Hill has $3,000 capital gain and a $0 basis. Ordinary treatment would require hot assets under §751.

questions.q: In complete liquidation of her interest, Irwin (outside basis $40,000) received $10,000 cash, inventory with a partnership basis of $8,000, and land with a partnership basis of $5,000 and fair market value of $20,000. What is Irwin's basis in the land?
questions.exp: In a liquidating distribution, basis is reduced by cash ($30,000 left), then inventory takes its carryover $8,000 ($22,000 left), and the land absorbs all remaining basis of $22,000 (§732, ). Using the partnership's $5,000 carryover basis is correct only for nonliquidating distributions.

questions.q: Jones, whose outside basis was $50,000, received $20,000 cash and inventory with a partnership basis of $15,000 in complete liquidation of his interest. What is the result to Jones?
choices: $15,000 capital loss, and a $15,000 basis in the inventory
No loss; the unused $15,000 of basis is suspended
No loss; the inventory takes a $30,000 basis
$15,000 ordinary loss, and a $15,000 basis in the inventory
questions.exp: When a liquidating distribution consists only of money, unrealized receivables and inventory, a loss is recognized to the extent basis exceeds the money plus the carryover basis of those items: $50,000 − $20,000 − $15,000 = $15,000 capital loss (§731). Inventory can never take a basis above the partnership's basis, so it cannot absorb the extra $15,000.

questions.q: King's outside basis in a partnership interest was $8,000, which included King's $10,000 share of partnership recourse liabilities. During the year the partnership paid off all its liabilities and had no other activity. The partnership holds no hot assets. What does King recognize?
choices: $2,000 ordinary income
Nothing, because King received no cash
$10,000 capital gain
$2,000 capital gain
questions.exp: A decrease in a partner's share of liabilities is a deemed distribution of money under §752; the $10,000 deemed distribution exceeds the $8,000 basis by $2,000, which is capital gain under §731. Overlooking the deemed distribution is the trap.

questions.q: Lee is a 30% partner who receives an annual guaranteed payment of $40,000 for services. The partnership's ordinary business income before deducting the guaranteed payment is $100,000. How much ordinary income does Lee report from the partnership for the year?
questions.exp: The guaranteed payment is deductible by the partnership (§707), leaving $60,000 of ordinary income, of which Lee's 30% share is $18,000; total = $40,000 + $18,000 = $58,000. Adding $40,000 to 30% of the pre-deduction $100,000 double counts.

questions.q: Moore contributed land with a basis of $10,000 and a fair market value of $30,000 to a partnership for a 50% interest. Two years later the partnership sold the land for $36,000. The partnership uses the traditional method under §704. How much of the gain is allocated to Moore?
questions.exp: The $20,000 precontribution built-in gain is allocated entirely to Moore under §704, and the $6,000 post-contribution appreciation is shared 50/50, giving Moore $20,000 + $3,000 = $23,000. Splitting the full $26,000 gain equally gives $13,000.

questions.q: Nash contributed land with a basis of $15,000 and a fair market value of $40,000 to a partnership. Three years later, when the land was worth $45,000, the partnership distributed it to another partner, Ortiz. What gain does Nash recognize?
choices: $0, because Nash received no distribution
questions.exp: Under the 'mixing bowl' rule of §704, when contributed property is distributed to another partner within seven years of contribution, the contributor recognizes the precontribution gain ($40,000 − $15,000 = $25,000). Post-contribution appreciation is not included.

questions.q: Perez sold her one-third partnership interest for $50,000 cash. Her basis was $30,000. The cash-basis partnership has accounts receivable with a zero basis, of which Perez's share is worth $12,000; it has no other hot assets or liabilities. How is Perez's $20,000 gain characterized?
choices: $12,000 capital gain and $8,000 ordinary income
$12,000 ordinary income and $8,000 capital gain
$20,000 capital gain
$20,000 ordinary income
questions.exp: Section 751 treats the amount attributable to unrealized receivables as ordinary income ($12,000); the remaining $8,000 is capital gain under §741. Treating the entire gain as capital ignores the hot-asset rule.

questions.q: Quinn sold his partnership interest to a new partner for $60,000 cash. Quinn's outside basis, including his $20,000 share of partnership liabilities, was $50,000. The buyer assumed Quinn's share of liabilities. The partnership has no hot assets. What gain does Quinn recognize?
questions.exp: Amount realized includes relief of liabilities: $60,000 + $20,000 = $80,000, less the $50,000 basis = $30,000 capital gain (§§741, 752). Comparing only the cash to a basis that includes liabilities understates the gain at $10,000.

questions.q: A newly formed partnership has three partners. Partners owning a combined 60% of profits and capital use a calendar year; the remaining partner, owning 40%, uses a June 30 fiscal year. Absent a business purpose or §444 election, what taxable year must the partnership use?
choices: The year producing the least aggregate deferral, computed without regard to majority ownership
Calendar year
Any fiscal year the partnership selects
June 30 fiscal year
questions.exp: Under §706, a partnership must first use the majority-interest taxable year (more than 50%), which is the calendar year here. The least-aggregate-deferral test applies only if there is no majority-interest year and no common year among principal partners.

questions.q: Ruiz contributed appreciated property to a partnership. Fourteen months later the partnership distributed cash to Ruiz. Absent facts clearly establishing otherwise, how are the transfers treated?
choices: As a guaranteed payment to Ruiz
As a nontaxable contribution because more than one year elapsed
As a presumed disguised sale of the property to the partnership
As a nontaxable contribution followed by a separate nontaxable distribution
questions.exp: Under §707 and the regulations, a contribution and a related distribution within two years are presumed to be a disguised sale unless the facts clearly establish otherwise. The one-year mark has no significance; the presumption window is two years.

questions.q: Smith owns a 60% capital and profits interest in a partnership. Smith sold land with a basis of $50,000 to the partnership for its fair market value of $35,000. Two years later the partnership sold the land to an unrelated party for $45,000. What gain does the partnership recognize on its sale?
choices: $5,000 loss
questions.exp: Smith's $15,000 loss was disallowed under §707 because Smith owns more than 50%; the partnership's later $10,000 gain is recognized only to the extent it exceeds the disallowed loss, so $0 is recognized. The disallowed loss cannot create a loss for the buyer.

questions.q: Which of the following increases a partner's basis in the partnership interest?
choices: The partner's distributive share of nondeductible, noncapital expenses
A cash distribution to the partner
An increase in the partner's share of partnership nonrecourse liabilities
The partner's share of the partnership's §179 expense
questions.exp: Under §752, an increase in a partner's share of any partnership liability, recourse or nonrecourse, is treated as a contribution of money that increases basis. Nondeductible expenses, distributions and §179 deductions all reduce basis.

questions.q: Taylor is a limited partner (not a general partner) in a partnership. During the year Taylor received a $10,000 guaranteed payment for services actually rendered to the partnership and was allocated a $25,000 distributive share of ordinary business income. How much is Taylor's net earnings from self-employment from the partnership?
questions.exp: Under §1402, a limited partner's distributive share is excluded from self-employment income, but guaranteed payments for services are included. A general partner would include both amounts.

questions.q: During the current year, partners holding a 60% interest in a partnership sold their interests to unrelated buyers. The business continues to be operated in partnership form. What is the effect on the partnership?
choices: The partnership's tax year closes for all partners on the sale date
The partnership technically terminates because more than 50% of the interests were sold within 12 months
The partnership does not terminate; its tax year closes only with respect to the selling partners
The partnership terminates only if the buyers were not existing partners
questions.exp: The technical termination rule of former §708 was repealed for tax years after 2017; a partnership terminates only if no part of its business continues in partnership form. A sale of a partner's entire interest closes the year only for that partner (§706).

questions.q: Underwood contributed land held as an investment for three years to a newly formed partnership. Five months later Underwood sold the partnership interest at a gain. The partnership holds no hot assets. How is Underwood's gain characterized?
choices: Ordinary income, because the interest was held less than one year
Short-term capital gain, because the interest was held only five months
Long-term capital gain, because the holding period of the land tacks to the interest
Section 1231 gain
questions.exp: A partner's holding period for an interest received for a capital or §1231 asset includes the holding period of the contributed property (§1223(1)). A holding period beginning on the contribution date applies to interests received for cash or ordinary-income property.

questions.q: Vance contributed business equipment with an adjusted basis of $20,000 and fair market value of $35,000 (original cost $50,000) to a partnership in exchange for an interest. What are the tax consequences of the contribution?
choices: Vance recognizes $15,000 of §1231 gain, and the partnership takes a $35,000 basis
No gain is recognized; the partnership takes a $20,000 basis and the recapture potential carries over
The partnership takes a $35,000 basis with no gain recognized by Vance
Vance recognizes $15,000 of §1245 ordinary income on the contribution
questions.exp: A contribution under §721 is nontaxable, and depreciation recapture is not triggered by a carryover-basis transfer (§1245); the partnership takes Vance's $20,000 basis and inherits the recapture potential. Recapture arises only on a later taxable disposition.

questions.q: In a nonliquidating distribution, a partner received inventory items from the partnership. Three years later the partner, who is not a dealer, sold the inventory at a gain. How is the gain characterized?
choices: Ordinary income
Capital gain only to the extent of appreciation after the distribution
Long-term capital gain, because the partner held the items more than one year
Section 1231 gain
questions.exp: Under §735, gain or loss on the sale of distributed inventory items within five years of the distribution is ordinary income or loss, regardless of how the partner holds them. The partner's own use as a capital asset matters only after five years.

questions.q: Wells purchased a partnership interest from a retiring partner for $100,000. Wells's share of the partnership's inside basis in its assets is $70,000. The partnership has a §754 election in effect. What basis adjustment results?
choices: A $30,000 increase in the basis of partnership assets, allocated among all partners
A $30,000 special basis adjustment to partnership assets with respect to Wells only
No adjustment, because the transaction was between partners and did not involve the partnership
A $70,000 increase to Wells's outside basis
questions.exp: With a §754 election, §743 gives the transferee a special basis adjustment equal to the difference between outside basis ($100,000) and the share of inside basis ($70,000), which benefits only the transferee. It does not change the other partners' shares of inside basis.

questions.q: At the beginning of the year Young's basis in a partnership interest was $10,000. During the year Young received a $6,000 cash distribution and was allocated a $12,000 share of the partnership's ordinary loss. There were no other items. How much of the loss may Young deduct for the year?
questions.exp: Basis is reduced by distributions before losses (Reg. §1.704-1): $10,000 − $6,000 = $4,000, so only $4,000 of loss is deductible and $8,000 is suspended. Applying the loss first would wrongly allow $10,000 and create $6,000 of distribution gain.

questions.q: A partnership began business on July 1 of the current year. It incurred $52,000 of organizational costs and $10,000 of syndication costs for selling partnership interests. Assuming the partnership elects to deduct and amortize the maximum allowed, what is its total deduction for these costs in the current year?
questions.exp: Under §709, the $5,000 immediate deduction is reduced by $2,000 (costs over $50,000) to $3,000, and the remaining $49,000 is amortized over 180 months: $49,000 / 180 × 6 = $1,633, for $4,633 total. Syndication costs are neither deductible nor amortizable, so including them is the trap.

questions.q: Which of the following items is separately stated on a partner's Schedule K-1 rather than included in the partnership's ordinary business income?
choices: Cost of goods sold
MACRS depreciation on business equipment (other than §179 expense)
Charitable contributions
Salaries paid to nonpartner employees
questions.exp: Items whose tax treatment may differ by partner, such as charitable contributions, are separately stated under §702. Employee salaries, regular depreciation and COGS are netted in ordinary business income.

questions.q: A partnership with three equal partners earned $90,000 of ordinary business income for the year and distributed $20,000 in cash to Zane, one of the partners. Zane's beginning basis was $40,000. How much partnership income must Zane report for the year?
questions.exp: Partners are taxed on their distributive share whether or not distributed (§702), so Zane reports one-third of $90,000 = $30,000. The $20,000 distribution is a nontaxable return of basis because it does not exceed Zane's basis.

topics.topic: Property transactions — basis and holding period

questions.q: Ada gave her nephew land with an adjusted basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $40,000. Assume the annual gift tax exclusion is $19,000, and Ada paid $4,200 of gift tax on the gift. What is the nephew's basis in the land?
questions.exp: Under §1015, the donee adds only the gift tax attributable to net appreciation: $4,200 x $20,000 / $21,000 taxable gift = $4,000, so basis is $20,000 + $4,000 = $24,000. Adding the full $4,200 gift tax gives $24,200.

questions.q: Bea received stock as a gift from her uncle when its fair market value was $7,000; the uncle's adjusted basis was $10,000. No gift tax was paid. Bea later sold the stock for $8,000. What gain or loss does Bea recognize?
choices: $3,000 loss
$1,000 gain
$2,000 loss
questions.exp: For gift property with value below the donor's basis, gain is measured from the donor's $10,000 basis and loss from the $7,000 value; a sale at $8,000 falls between the two and produces no gain or loss. Using the donor's basis alone yields the $2,000 loss.

questions.q: Cal received shares as a gift when their fair market value was $7,000; the donor had held them for three years and had a $10,000 basis. Four months after the gift, Cal sold the shares for $5,000. What is the amount and character of Cal's loss?
choices: $5,000 long-term capital loss
$2,000 long-term capital loss
$5,000 short-term capital loss
$2,000 short-term capital loss
questions.exp: Loss basis is the $7,000 fair market value at the gift, so the loss is $2,000, and because the fair-value basis is used, the holding period starts on the date of the gift, making the loss short-term. Tacking the donor's three-year holding period is allowed only when the donor's basis is used.

questions.q: Dan inherited stock from his aunt, whose basis was $20,000. The stock was worth $50,000 at her death, and the executor did not elect alternate valuation. Two months after her death Dan sold the stock for $53,000. What gain does Dan recognize?
choices: $3,000 short-term
$3,000 long-term
$33,000 short-term
$33,000 long-term
questions.exp: Inherited property takes a basis equal to fair market value at death ($50,000) under §1014, and its holding period is automatically long-term, so the gain is a $3,000 long-term gain. Using the decedent's basis gives $33,000.

questions.q: Eli died owning a building worth $100,000; his basis was $40,000. The executor elected the alternate valuation date. Four months after death, when the building was worth $90,000, the executor distributed it to Eli's daughter. Six months after death it would have been worth $85,000. What is the daughter's basis in the building?
questions.exp: When alternate valuation is elected, property distributed or sold within six months of death is valued on the date of distribution ($90,000). The six-month value of $85,000 applies only to property still held by the estate on that date.

questions.q: Finn gave his father stock with a basis of $10,000 and a fair market value of $50,000. Eight months later his father died, leaving the stock to Finn; it was then worth $60,000. What is Finn's basis in the inherited stock?
questions.exp: Under §1014, no step-up applies to appreciated property acquired by the decedent by gift within one year of death that passes back to the donor; Finn's basis is the father's $10,000 adjusted basis. Using the $60,000 date-of-death value ignores this anti-abuse rule.

questions.q: Gia bought a rental building by paying $100,000 cash and assuming the seller's $300,000 mortgage. She also paid $5,000 of title, legal and recording fees on the purchase. What is Gia's basis in the building?
questions.exp: Cost basis includes cash paid, liabilities assumed and acquisition costs such as title and legal fees: $100,000 + $300,000 + $5,000 = $405,000. Omitting the assumed mortgage gives $105,000.

questions.q: Hal paid $500,000 for land and a building to be used in his business. At the purchase date the land was appraised at $150,000 and the building at $450,000. What is Hal's basis in the building?
questions.exp: A lump-sum price is allocated by relative fair market values: $500,000 x $450,000 / $600,000 = $375,000. Subtracting the land's full appraised value from the price gives $350,000.

questions.q: Ivan sold 100 shares of stock with a basis of $10,000 for $8,000 on December 1. On December 21 he bought 100 shares of the same stock for $8,500. What is Ivan's basis in the newly acquired shares?
questions.exp: Under the §1091 wash sale rule the $2,000 loss is disallowed and added to the basis of the replacement shares: $8,500 + $2,000 = $10,500. Using the $8,500 cost ignores the deferred loss.

questions.q: Jon sold stock with a basis of $20,000 to his sister for $12,000, its fair market value. Two years later, his sister sold the stock to an unrelated buyer for $17,000. What gain or loss does the sister recognize?
choices: $5,000 gain
$8,000 loss
$3,000 loss
questions.exp: Jon's $8,000 loss is disallowed under §267, but the sister may use it to offset her later gain: her $5,000 gain ($17,000 - $12,000) is reduced to $0; the unused $3,000 is lost. A related buyer can never deduct the seller's disallowed loss, so a $3,000 loss is not allowed.

questions.q: Kim's aunt gave her stock the aunt had held for 10 months; its fair market value at the gift exceeded the aunt's basis. Kim sold the stock at a gain three months after receiving it. What is the character of Kim's gain?
choices: Long-term, because the donor's holding period tacks on
Long-term, because all gift property is treated as held more than one year
Short-term, because gift property always starts a new holding period
Short-term, because Kim held it only three months
questions.exp: When the donee takes the donor's basis, the donor's holding period is added, giving 13 months and a long-term gain. Only inherited property is automatically long-term.

questions.q: Lou owns 100 shares of common stock with a total basis of $12,000. He receives a nontaxable distribution of 20 additional common shares as a stock dividend. What is Lou's basis per share after the distribution?
choices: $0 for the new shares and $120 for the old shares
questions.exp: Under §307, the original basis is spread over all shares held after a nontaxable stock dividend: $12,000 / 120 = $100 per share. Giving the new shares zero basis is the trap.

questions.q: Mae owns stock with a basis of $20,000 and a fair market value of $40,000. She receives nontaxable stock rights with a fair market value of $2,000 and makes no election regarding basis. What basis do the rights receive?
choices: $2,000, the rights' fair market value
$952, a required allocation by relative values
questions.exp: If the rights are worth less than 15% of the stock's value ($2,000 / $40,000 = 5%), their basis is zero unless the shareholder elects to allocate. The $952 figure would apply only if the election were made.

questions.q: Ned converted his former residence to rental property. At conversion the building's adjusted basis was $200,000 and its fair market value was $160,000 (ignore land). What is Ned's basis for depreciation?
questions.exp: Property converted from personal to business use is depreciated on the lesser of adjusted basis or fair market value at conversion ($160,000). Using the $200,000 basis would let a nondeductible personal decline in value be deducted.

questions.q: When Ned converted his residence to a rental, the building's adjusted basis was $200,000 and its fair market value $160,000 (ignore land). After claiming $10,000 of depreciation, he sold the building for $140,000. What gain or loss does Ned recognize?
questions.exp: For loss, basis is the lower fair market value at conversion less depreciation: $160,000 - $10,000 = $150,000, giving a $10,000 loss. Using the original $200,000 basis less depreciation yields the $50,000 loss, which includes the pre-conversion personal decline.

questions.q: Opal sold her personal car, which cost $30,000, for $18,000. She also sold a painting she had owned for several years and kept in her home, with a basis of $10,000, for $15,000. What net gain or loss does Opal recognize?
choices: $5,000 gain
$3,000 loss
$7,000 loss
questions.exp: Gain on personal-use assets is a taxable capital gain ($5,000), but loss on personal-use assets such as a personal car is not deductible, so the two cannot be netted. Netting them gives the $7,000 loss.

questions.q: Pat bought stock on March 10, Year 1. What is the earliest date Pat can sell the stock and have the gain treated as long-term?
choices: March 11, Year 2
March 11, Year 3
September 10, Year 1
March 10, Year 2
questions.exp: Long-term status requires holding for more than one year; the holding period starts the day after acquisition, so a sale on March 11, Year 2 qualifies. A sale on March 10, Year 2 is exactly one year and is short-term.

questions.q: Quin traded land held for investment (basis $30,000, fair market value $50,000) for a boat with a fair market value of $50,000 that he will use for personal recreation. What is Quin's basis in the boat?
questions.exp: The exchange is taxable because the boat is not held for investment or business use, so Quin recognizes $20,000 of gain and takes a fair market value (cost) basis of $50,000. A carryover $30,000 basis would apply only in a like-kind exchange.

questions.q: Rae's employer sold her land worth $80,000 for $50,000 as compensation for services. What is Rae's basis in the land?
questions.exp: Rae recognizes $30,000 of compensation income on the bargain purchase, and her basis is the $50,000 paid plus the $30,000 included in income, or $80,000. Using only the price paid would tax the $30,000 twice.

questions.q: Sid bought his home for $300,000. He later added a family room for $40,000, repainted the interior for $3,000, and claimed $5,000 of depreciation for a qualifying home office. What is Sid's adjusted basis in the home?
questions.exp: Basis is increased by capital improvements and reduced by depreciation, while repairs such as painting are not added: $300,000 + $40,000 - $5,000 = $335,000. Adding the painting gives $338,000.

questions.q: Tess bought 100 shares of Q Corp. for $20 per share in January, Year 1, and another 100 shares for $30 per share in June, Year 1. In December, Year 2, she sold 100 shares for $35 per share without identifying which shares were sold. What is her recognized gain?
questions.exp: Absent specific identification, the first shares acquired are treated as sold first: 100 x ($35 - $20) = $1,500. The $1,000 figure uses average cost, which applies to mutual fund shares, not individual stock by default.

questions.q: Incident to their divorce, Uma's husband transferred to her stock with a basis of $30,000 and a fair market value of $70,000. Uma later sold the stock for $75,000. What gain does Uma recognize?
questions.exp: Under §1041, transfers incident to divorce are treated as gifts: no gain to the transferor and a carryover basis of $30,000 to Uma, so her gain is $75,000 - $30,000 = $45,000. Using the $70,000 value gives $5,000.

questions.q: Val sold land with a fair market value of $100,000 and a basis of $40,000 to his son for $30,000, intending the difference as a gift. What is the son's basis in the land, ignoring any gift tax?
questions.exp: In a part-gift, part-sale, the donee's basis is the greater of the amount paid ($30,000) or the donor's adjusted basis ($40,000). The seller realizes no gain because $30,000 does not exceed his basis.

questions.q: Wyn's business equipment cost $50,000. Depreciation allowable through the date of sale was $30,000, but Wyn claimed only $20,000. He sold the equipment for $25,000. What gain or loss does Wyn recognize?
choices: $5,000 loss
$5,000 gain
questions.exp: Basis is reduced by the greater of depreciation allowed or allowable, so adjusted basis is $50,000 - $30,000 = $20,000 and the gain is $5,000. Reducing basis only by the $20,000 claimed gives a $5,000 loss.

questions.q: Xavi sold investment land with a basis of $50,000. The buyer paid $40,000 cash and assumed Xavi's $60,000 mortgage on the land. Xavi paid $5,000 of selling commissions. What is Xavi's recognized gain?
questions.exp: Amount realized includes liabilities assumed by the buyer and is reduced by selling costs: $40,000 + $60,000 - $5,000 = $95,000, less $50,000 basis = $45,000. Ignoring the assumed mortgage produces a $10,000 loss.

questions.q: Yuki bought 100 shares of stock three years ago. Six months ago she received 10 additional shares as a nontaxable stock dividend, and today she sold those 10 shares at a gain. What is the character of the gain?
choices: Short-term, because nontaxable distributions start a new holding period
Short-term, because the dividend shares were received six months ago
Long-term, because the holding period of the new shares includes that of the original shares
Ordinary income, because the shares were received as a dividend
questions.exp: Shares received in a nontaxable stock dividend take a holding period that includes the holding period of the underlying stock, so the gain is long-term. Starting a new holding period at the distribution date is the trap.

questions.q: Zed and his wife, residents of a community property state, owned their home as community property with a total basis of $200,000. When Zed died, the home was worth $600,000. What is the surviving wife's basis in the home?
questions.exp: When a spouse dies, both halves of community property receive a basis equal to fair market value at death if at least half is included in the decedent's estate, giving $600,000. The $400,000 figure applies the common-law rule of stepping up only the decedent's half.

questions.q: On August 1, Year 1, Ari bought stock for $8,000. In March, Year 2, the corporation went bankrupt and the stock became totally worthless. How does Ari treat the loss?
choices: As an ordinary loss
As a long-term capital loss, because worthless securities are treated as sold on the last day of the year
No loss is allowed until the stock is sold
As a short-term capital loss, because the stock became worthless less than a year after purchase
questions.exp: Under §165, a security that becomes worthless is treated as sold on the last day of the tax year (December 31, Year 2), giving a holding period over one year and a long-term capital loss. Measuring to the date of worthlessness gives the short-term answer.

questions.q: A building with an adjusted basis of $100,000 was partially damaged by fire. Insurance paid $20,000, and the owner deducted a $15,000 casualty loss for the unreimbursed damage. The owner then spent $30,000 restoring the building. What is the building's adjusted basis after the restoration?
questions.exp: Basis is reduced by insurance received and by the deductible loss, then increased by restoration costs: $100,000 - $20,000 - $15,000 + $30,000 = $95,000. Forgetting to reduce basis by the deducted loss gives $110,000.

questions.q: Bree bought a home for $400,000. The seller paid $4,000 of points on Bree's new mortgage, and Bree paid $3,000 of title insurance and recording fees. What is Bree's basis in the home?
questions.exp: Settlement costs such as title insurance increase basis, and seller-paid points are treated as paid by the buyer (deductible by her) but reduce her basis: $400,000 + $3,000 - $4,000 = $399,000. Ignoring the seller-paid points gives $403,000.

questions.q: For purposes of the 100-shareholder limit on S corporations, how are members of a family treated?
choices: Family members count as one shareholder only if they live in the same household
Only a husband and wife may be treated as one shareholder
All members of a family, including lineal descendants of a common ancestor and their spouses, are treated as one shareholder
Each family member always counts as a separate shareholder
questions.exp: Members of a family (a common ancestor, lineal descendants within six generations, and their spouses and former spouses) are treated as one shareholder for the 100-shareholder limit. The rule is broader than the spousal rule alone.

questions.q: Which of the following may be a shareholder of an S corporation?
choices: A C corporation
A partnership
A nonresident alien individual
The estate of a deceased individual
questions.exp: Eligible shareholders are generally U.S. citizen or resident individuals, estates, and certain trusts and exempt organizations. Partnerships, corporations and nonresident aliens are ineligible, and any one of them owning shares disqualifies the corporation.

questions.q: Cam Corp. has two classes of common stock that are identical in rights to distributions and liquidation proceeds, except that one class has voting rights and the other does not. May Cam elect S status?
choices: Yes, because differences solely in voting rights do not create a second class of stock
No, unless the nonvoting shares are held by a single shareholder
Yes, but only if the nonvoting shares are less than 20% of the total
No, because it has more than one class of stock
questions.exp: An S corporation may have only one class of stock, but shares that differ only in voting rights are disregarded for that test. A true second class arises from differing rights to distributions or liquidation proceeds.

questions.q: Dew Corp., a calendar-year C corporation, wants S status for the current year. It has had the same shareholders since January 1, and all of them consent. What is the latest date it may file Form 2553 for the election to be effective as of January 1 of the current year, absent relief for a late election?
choices: April 15 of the current year
The due date of the current year's return
December 31 of the current year
March 15 of the current year
questions.exp: An election made by the 15th day of the third month of the tax year (March 15 for a calendar year) can be effective for that year; a later election takes effect the following year unless late-election relief applies. The return due date is not the election deadline.

questions.q: Eve owns 40% of an S corporation. Her stock basis at the beginning of the year was $10,000. For the year her share of items was: ordinary business income $25,000, tax-exempt interest $2,000, nondeductible expenses $1,000, and cash distributions $15,000. What is her stock basis at year-end?
questions.exp: Basis = $10,000 + $25,000 + $2,000 − $15,000 − $1,000 = $21,000. Tax-exempt income increases basis and nondeductible expenses decrease it; ignoring the tax-exempt interest gives $19,000 and ignoring the nondeductible expense gives $22,000.

questions.q: Finn has an $8,000 basis in his S corporation stock and has lent the corporation $5,000. His share of the corporation's ordinary loss for the year is $20,000. How much of the loss may Finn deduct this year, assuming the at-risk and passive activity rules do not limit it?
questions.exp: Losses are deductible first against stock basis ($8,000) and then against basis in loans the shareholder made directly to the corporation ($5,000), for $13,000; the remaining $7,000 is suspended and carried forward indefinitely. Stopping at stock basis gives $8,000.

questions.q: Gil, the sole shareholder of an S corporation, personally guaranteed a $100,000 bank loan made to the corporation. The corporation has not defaulted. What effect does the guarantee have on Gil's basis for deducting losses?
choices: It increases his debt basis by $100,000
It increases his basis by his pro rata share of the loan
It has no effect until Gil actually makes payments on the guarantee
It increases his stock basis by $100,000
questions.exp: A shareholder's guarantee of an entity loan does not create debt basis; only loans the shareholder makes directly to the S corporation (or payments made under the guarantee) count. Unlike a partnership, an S corporation's liabilities do not flow into shareholder basis.

questions.q: In a prior year, Hana's basis in a loan to her S corporation was reduced by passed-through losses. This year the corporation has net income. How is the net increase applied?
choices: Pro rata between stock basis and debt basis
It is ignored until the loan is repaid
To restore debt basis first, then to increase stock basis
Entirely to stock basis
questions.exp: A net increase in a later year first restores the reduced basis of the shareholder's loan (up to its face amount) and then increases stock basis. Restoring debt basis first matters because repayment of a loan with reduced basis produces gain.

questions.q: An S corporation with a 365-day calendar year had ordinary business income of $365,000, earned evenly. Ann owned all 100 shares until she sold 50 shares to Ben, who is treated as owning them for the last 219 days of the year. No election to close the books was made. What is Ben's share of the ordinary income?
questions.exp: Absent an election, items are allocated per share, per day: $365,000 ÷ 365 = $1,000 per day × 50% × 219 days = $109,500. Allocating half of the full year's income ($182,500) ignores that Ben owned shares for only part of the year.

questions.q: Ivo is the sole shareholder of an S corporation that has never been a C corporation. After adjusting for the current year's income, his stock basis is $12,000. The corporation distributes $20,000 cash to him. How does Ivo treat the distribution?
choices: $12,000 tax-free and $8,000 capital gain
$20,000 tax-free, with a negative basis of $8,000
$12,000 dividend and $8,000 return of capital
$20,000 dividend income
questions.exp: An S corporation with no accumulated E&P makes distributions that are tax-free to the extent of stock basis, and the excess, $20,000 − $12,000 = $8,000, is treated as gain from the sale of the stock. Basis cannot go below zero.

questions.q: Jett Corp., an S corporation that was formerly a C corporation, has an accumulated adjustments account of $10,000 and accumulated E&P of $6,000. Its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $30,000, receives a $20,000 cash distribution. How much of the distribution is a taxable dividend?
questions.exp: Distributions come first from AAA ($10,000 tax-free, reducing basis), then from accumulated E&P ($6,000 dividend), and the last $4,000 is a tax-free return of basis. Concluding $0 because basis exceeds the distribution ignores the accumulated E&P layer.

questions.q: Kilo Corp. converted from a C corporation to an S corporation three years ago. This year it sold an asset it owned on the conversion date and recognized a $50,000 net built-in gain, and the taxable income limitation does not reduce that amount. What built-in gains tax does Kilo owe?
questions.exp: Built-in gains recognized within five years after conversion are taxed to the S corporation at the 21% corporate rate: 21% × $50,000 = $10,500. Answering $0 assumes S corporations never pay entity-level income tax.

questions.q: An S corporation's election terminates because of excess passive investment income when the corporation:
choices: Has passive investment income exceeding 25% of gross receipts in any single year
Has accumulated E&P from C corporation years at the end of each of three consecutive tax years and passive investment income exceeding 25% of gross receipts in each of those years
Has any passive investment income while it has accumulated E&P
Has passive investment income exceeding 50% of gross receipts for two consecutive years
questions.exp: Termination requires three consecutive years in which the corporation both has accumulated C corporation E&P at year-end and passive investment income exceeding 25% of gross receipts. A single year produces only the excess net passive income tax, not termination.

questions.q: On July 1 of the current year, a shareholder of a calendar-year S corporation sold some of her shares to a partnership. What is the effect on the S election?
choices: The election continues if the partnership's partners are all individuals
The election terminates at the beginning of the current year
The election terminates on July 1, so the S short year ends June 30
The election terminates on January 1 of the following year
questions.exp: When a corporation ceases to qualify, the election terminates on the date of the disqualifying event, and the day before is the last day of the S short year; a C short year follows. A partnership is an ineligible shareholder regardless of who its partners are.

questions.q: A calendar-year S corporation has 1,000 shares outstanding, 400 of them nonvoting. Which group of shareholders may revoke the S election?
choices: Shareholders owning more than 50% of the voting shares only
Shareholders owning at least two-thirds of all shares
Shareholders owning more than 50% of all outstanding shares, voting and nonvoting
All shareholders unanimously
questions.exp: A revocation requires consent of shareholders holding more than one-half of the outstanding shares, counting both voting and nonvoting stock. Unanimous consent is required to make an election, not to revoke one.

questions.q: After an S election is terminated or revoked, how long must the corporation generally wait before making a new S election without IRS consent?
choices: One year
Three years
Until the fifth tax year beginning after the first year for which the termination was effective
No waiting period applies
questions.exp: A corporation whose election terminated generally may not re-elect S status for five tax years unless the IRS consents. The one-year figure is a confusion with the post-termination transition period.

questions.q: Which item of an S corporation is NOT separately stated on the shareholders' Schedules K-1?
choices: Net long-term capital gain
Charitable contributions
Depreciation on business equipment, other than §179 expense
Tax-exempt interest income
questions.exp: Ordinary depreciation enters the computation of nonseparately stated ordinary business income. Charitable contributions, capital gains and tax-exempt income are separately stated because they may affect each shareholder's tax differently.

questions.q: An S corporation pays health insurance premiums for Lin, an employee who owns 10% of its stock. How are the premiums treated?
choices: Excluded from Lin's income as a tax-free employee fringe benefit
Nondeductible by the corporation and treated as a distribution to Lin
Deductible by the corporation and included in Lin's wages, with Lin generally eligible for the self-employed health insurance deduction
Deductible by the corporation and exempt from income tax withholding and reporting
questions.exp: A more-than-2% shareholder is treated like a partner for fringe benefit purposes, so premiums paid on his behalf are included in his W-2 wages (though not subject to FICA under these rules), and he may generally deduct them as self-employed health insurance. Tax-free fringe treatment applies only to employees owning 2% or less.

questions.q: Moe is the sole shareholder and only employee of a profitable S corporation. He takes no salary and withdraws all profits as distributions. What is the most likely result if the IRS examines the corporation?
choices: The S election will terminate
The distributions will be taxed as dividends at ordinary rates
No change, because S corporation distributions are never subject to payroll taxes
The IRS may recharacterize a portion as reasonable wages subject to employment taxes
questions.exp: A shareholder-employee who performs substantial services must be paid reasonable compensation, and the IRS can recharacterize distributions as wages subject to FICA and withholding. Avoiding employment tax does not terminate the election or create dividends.

questions.q: Nan's S corporation stock basis at the beginning of the year was $10,000. For the year, her share of the ordinary loss was $12,000, and she received a $6,000 cash distribution. There were no income items. How much of the loss may she deduct this year?
questions.exp: Basis is reduced by distributions before losses, so the $6,000 distribution is tax-free and leaves $4,000 of basis, which limits the loss deduction to $4,000; the remaining $8,000 is suspended. Applying the loss first would deduct $10,000 and make the distribution taxable.

questions.q: Which statement about an S corporation's tax year is correct?
choices: It must use a fiscal year ending in September
It must use the tax year of its largest shareholder, even if that is a fiscal year
It must use a calendar year unless it establishes a business purpose for a fiscal year or makes a §444 election
It may adopt any fiscal year without restriction
questions.exp: An S corporation must use a permitted year, which is the calendar year unless it establishes a business purpose (such as a natural business year) or elects a fiscal year under §444 with required payments. Free choice of fiscal year is a C corporation rule.

questions.q: Which of the following taxes may be imposed on an S corporation itself?
choices: Corporate alternative minimum tax on adjusted financial statement income
Built-in gains tax
Personal holding company tax
Accumulated earnings tax
questions.exp: An S corporation can owe entity-level tax on built-in gains, excess net passive income and LIFO recapture. The accumulated earnings and personal holding company taxes apply only to C corporations.

questions.q: Ora formed an S corporation by transferring land with an adjusted basis of $40,000 and a fair market value of $70,000 for all of its stock in a transaction qualifying under §351. What is Ora's initial stock basis?
questions.exp: S corporations are formed under the same §351 rules as C corporations, so Ora takes a substituted basis equal to the land's $40,000 basis. Fair market value would be used only if the exchange were taxable.

questions.q: Pax had $15,000 of S corporation losses suspended for lack of basis when the corporation's S election terminated. How may Pax use the suspended losses?
choices: They are deductible to the extent Pax increases stock basis by the end of the post-termination transition period
They are lost when the election terminates
They may be deducted only against future C corporation dividends
They convert to a capital loss carryover
questions.exp: Suspended losses are treated as incurred on the last day of the post-termination transition period (generally one year after the last S day, or later through the final return's extended due date), so Pax can deduct them by restoring stock basis, such as by contributing capital, before that period ends. Otherwise they are lost.

questions.q: In applying limitations to an S corporation shareholder's share of a loss, what is the correct order?
choices: Passive activity rules, then at-risk rules, then basis limitation
Basis limitation, then passive activity rules, then at-risk rules
At-risk rules, then basis limitation, then passive activity rules
Basis limitation, then at-risk rules, then passive activity rules
questions.exp: A loss must first clear the shareholder's stock and debt basis, then the at-risk rules of §465, and then the passive activity rules of §469 (with the excess business loss limit applied after that). Each limit applies only to the loss that survived the prior one.

questions.q: Which statement about S corporations and subsidiaries is correct?
choices: An S corporation may own stock of a C corporation only if it owns less than 50%
A subsidiary owned by an S corporation automatically shares the parent's S election
An S corporation may not own stock of any other corporation
An S corporation may own 100% of a qualified subchapter S subsidiary, which is disregarded as a separate entity
questions.exp: An S corporation may elect QSub treatment for a domestic corporation it wholly owns, and the QSub's items are treated as the parent's. It may also own any percentage of a C corporation; QSub status requires an election.

questions.q: Which corporation is NOT eligible to elect S status?
choices: A domestic corporation with 75 shareholders, all U.S. citizens
A foreign corporation
A domestic corporation owned by a grantor trust
A domestic corporation that was a C corporation last year
questions.exp: Only a domestic corporation that is not an ineligible corporation (such as certain financial institutions and insurance companies) may elect S status. A former C corporation and one owned by a grantor trust can qualify.

questions.q: Quin's basis in his S corporation stock was $50,000 on January 1. He sold all of his shares on September 30 for $80,000. His share of the corporation's ordinary income through September 30 was $10,000, and he received no distributions. What is his gain on the sale?
questions.exp: Basis is first increased by his $10,000 share of income through the sale date to $60,000, so gain = $80,000 − $60,000 = $20,000. Using the January 1 basis gives $30,000 and taxes the $10,000 of income twice.

questions.q: Rae owns 50% of an S corporation and works full-time in its business. How is her $60,000 share of the corporation's ordinary business income treated for employment tax purposes?
choices: It is subject to FICA withholding by the corporation
It is subject to self-employment tax because she materially participates
It is subject to self-employment tax only above her salary
It is not subject to self-employment tax
questions.exp: An S corporation shareholder's share of ordinary business income is not self-employment income; employment taxes apply only to wages actually paid. This differs from a general partner's distributive share, which is subject to SE tax.

questions.q: Which statement about the accumulated adjustments account (AAA) of an S corporation is correct?
choices: It is increased by tax-exempt income
It cannot become negative under any circumstances
It is maintained separately for each shareholder, like stock basis
It can become negative because of losses, but distributions cannot reduce it below zero
questions.exp: The AAA is a corporate-level account that is increased by income items other than tax-exempt income and decreased by losses and deductions, which can make it negative; distributions, however, cannot push it below zero. Stock basis, by contrast, is a shareholder-level figure that cannot go below zero.

questions.q: Under UCC Article 9, which of the following is NOT a requirement for a security interest to attach to collateral that the secured party does not possess or control?
choices: The debtor must authenticate a security agreement that describes the collateral
The secured party must give value
The secured party must file a financing statement
